courses.title: Promote Primary & Secondary Domain Controller
courses.subtitle: DC01 + DC02 / Active Directory
courses.description: Promote the primary and secondary domain controllers on Windows Server, place them on their own network segment, verify the domain's health, and keep a record of the build.

materials.title: Interactive build guide
materials.description: Explore the build and keep your evidence record.

materials.title: Training materials · ZIP
materials.description: Offline guide, workbook (PDF and Word), and verification commands.

lessons.title: Give every system a purpose
lessons.summary: Record the starting configuration, place both controllers on their own segment, and explain what they will do.

sections.heading: Understand the why
sections.body: Start by understanding the services you are about to build and where they will live. Then record the names, addresses, and dependencies for two controllers in the same domain.

sections.heading: What is Active Directory?
sections.body: The shared directory behind domain identities.

sections.heading: A directory for people and computers
sections.body: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the Windows Server directory service. It stores objects such as user accounts, computer accounts, and groups, together with their attributes. Administrators use this shared directory to organize identities and manage access consistently.

sections.heading: The domain and the controller
sections.body: A domain is a logical collection of directory objects, named here sbd.test. A domain controller (DC) is a server running AD DS that stores and serves that directory. DC01 and DC02 are two servers serving the same domain. A forest contains one or more domains; this build starts with one.

sections.heading: Identity, permissions, and policy
sections.body: Authentication checks who is signing in. Authorization determines what that identity may access. Signing in successfully does not grant access to every resource: the destination service still applies its permissions. Groups make it practical to assign access to roles instead of managing every person separately.

sections.heading: Organization and consistent settings
sections.body: Organizational units (OUs) organize objects and support delegated administration and Group Policy. Group Policy applies centrally managed settings to users and computers. A global catalog helps find directory objects across a forest; both controllers in this course provide that role.

sections.heading: Remember
sections.body: AD DS stores the directory, and every domain controller serves it. Authentication proves who someone is; authorization decides what they may reach.

sections.heading: Where do the controllers live?
sections.body: On a segment of their own, behind a core that denies by default.

sections.heading: A segment reserved for controllers
sections.body: SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 sit on VLAN 10 (10.0.10.0/24), a segment that holds domain controllers and nothing else. Workstations, member servers, security tools, and administrators sit on segments of their own. The core joins the segments, and its VLAN 10 address, 10.0.10.1, is the controllers' default gateway.

sections.heading: Deny by default, allow by exception
sections.body: The core denies every session between segments unless a documented rule permits it, and logs what it denies. Members reach the controllers only for name resolution (course 1.2), the services in "What crosses the network?", and course 1.8's credentialed scans. Traffic between the two controllers stays inside VLAN 10, so the core never routes it.

sections.heading: Only Tier 0 manages a controller
sections.body: From other segments, Remote Desktop, PowerShell remoting, and AD Web Services reach a controller only from AdminJumpBox01, the Tier 0 host on VLAN 60 that course 1.5 builds; until then, use the VM console. Members still reach SMB and RPC, which can carry administration too, so Tier 0 accounts never sign in to them.

sections.heading: Two layers, and no internet
sections.body: Windows Defender Firewall stays on in every profile and blocks what no rule allows, so an unopened port stays closed even if a core rule is wrong. Keep Remote Desktop off. The directory rules accept any address, and the remoting and AD Web Services rules do too until course 1.5 limits them to the Tier 0 host, so the core decides who reaches those ports. No segment routes to the internet; approved media is the only way in.

sections.heading: Remember
sections.body: A controller's segment is part of its security: VLAN 10 for controllers only, default deny at the core, management only from Tier 0, and the host firewall on in every profile.

sections.heading: Prepare two separate VMs
sections.body: Use new, patched Windows Server installations (Desktop Experience) with console access and the required administrative credentials. Connect both to VLAN 10, the segment reserved for domain controllers; nothing else joins it. Obtain approved media and updates through your established offline process.

sections.heading: Record names and addresses
sections.body: Rename the servers SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 and restart as needed. Use 10.0.10.10/24 and 10.0.10.11/24 with 10.0.10.1, the core's VLAN 10 address, as the default gateway. Every other segment reaches the controllers only through the core, which denies anything a rule doesn't permit.

sections.heading: Point DC02 at DC01 and check the clocks
sections.body: Set SBD-DC02's preferred Domain Name System (DNS) server to 10.0.10.10 so it can find the domain when you promote it, and leave it that way; course 1.2 explains the DNS design. Confirm both clocks agree and document the intended internal time source.

sections.heading: Inspect each server before promotion
sections.body:
hostname
Get-NetIPConfiguration
w32tm /query /status

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: The two names and static addresses match your plan, the default gateway is 10.0.10.1, and SBD-DC02 lists 10.0.10.10 as its DNS server. Record actual time-source output; a configured address alone does not prove time synchronization.

sections.heading: Avoid this mistake
sections.body: Renaming a domain controller later is a separate procedure with its own steps and checks. Set each server's final name and static address before you promote it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record your VM names, OS builds, addresses, segment and gateway, time source, and any differences from the sample.

quizzes.question: Why set each server's final name and static address before promotion?
answers: Changing them on a domain controller later is a separate procedure
Promotion assigns a name and address automatically
The domain takes its name from the first server's hostname
quizzes.explanation: Promotion records the server as a domain controller under its current name. Settle the name and address first; renaming a controller later has its own procedure and checks.

lessons.title: Create the first domain controller
lessons.summary: Create the sample forest and bring AD DS online on DC01.

sections.heading: Understand the why
sections.body: A new forest establishes the directory's initial boundary. Here, sbd.test is a sample domain, not an existing company domain. Follow this path only for a new forest.

sections.heading: Add the server role
sections.body: On DC01, open Server Manager → Manage → Add Roles and Features. Choose the local server and Active Directory Domain Services, including its management tools.

sections.heading: Create the forest
sections.body: Select Promote this server to a domain controller, then Add a new forest. Enter sbd.test. Because both controllers run the same Windows Server release, select the highest forest and domain functional levels the wizard offers. Leave the DNS server option selected; the wizard's DNS delegation warning is expected, and course 1.2 explains both. The first controller in a forest is always a global catalog. Enter and confirm a unique Directory Services Restore Mode password on the server.

sections.heading: Review and promote
sections.body: Review the SBD NetBIOS name, paths, and prerequisite results. Read any warnings, resolve blocking errors, install, and allow the restart. Then inspect the services and domain.

sections.heading: Verify DC01 after the restart
sections.body:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Get-Service NTDS,Netlogon
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: The domain is sbd.test with NetBIOS name SBD. NTDS and Netlogon are running, and SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares exist. Investigate missing services or shares before moving on.

sections.heading: Avoid this mistake
sections.body: Installing the AD DS role is only the first part. The promotion wizard creates the domain controller; a completed role installation alone is not a completed forest.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the domain, promotion outcome, service checks, and the file names of your screenshots or saved output. Do not enter passwords.

quizzes.question: What turns an AD DS role installation into a domain controller?
answers: Renaming the server
Completing domain-controller promotion
Adding a second network adapter
quizzes.explanation: Promotion configures the directory role for a new forest or an existing domain. Merely adding the role is insufficient.

lessons.title: Give the domain a second service point
lessons.summary: Promote DC02 into the existing domain and inspect the replication relationship.

sections.heading: Understand the why
sections.body: A second domain controller gives the domain another live service point. Read why this is a standard availability practice, then add DC02 and verify the result.

sections.heading: Why use two domain controllers?
sections.body: Keep the directory available when one server is unavailable.

sections.heading: Remove the single-server dependency
sections.body: With one DC, its outage removes the only live directory service point. With two healthy, reachable controllers, clients can use a surviving DC for supported operations. This also lets you patch or restart one server while the other continues serving requests. Reconnection may take time; uninterrupted service is not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Both controllers do useful work
sections.body: Both writable DCs can process normal directory changes and authentication requests. Replication shares directory changes between them. “Primary” and “secondary” describe the order you promote them, not a primary server and an idle spare. Certain operations still depend on a single FSMO role holder, so role placement and recovery need their own plan.

sections.heading: Make the redundancy real
sections.body: Microsoft recommends at least two virtualized DCs per domain on different virtualization hosts. Two VMs on one host share that host as a failure point. Consider shared storage, power, and network dependencies too.

sections.heading: Availability still needs recovery
sections.body: Replication can spread an accidental deletion or harmful change to both servers. Keep protected backups and test recovery separately. Two is a starting point for this design, not a universal capacity target: additional sites, users, and recovery needs may require more controllers.

sections.heading: Remember
sections.body: Before relying on DC02, verify replication, review shared dependencies, and confirm both controllers pass their health checks.

sections.heading: Reach the existing directory
sections.body: On DC02, check that DC01 answers at 10.0.10.10 and that both clocks agree before promotion.

sections.heading: Add a controller to this domain
sections.body: Install the AD DS role and management tools. In the promotion wizard choose Add a domain controller to an existing domain, enter sbd.test, and authenticate with an authorized Domain Admin account. Leave the DNS server and global catalog options selected, leave Read only domain controller unselected, and set the DSRM password securely.

sections.heading: Finish and inspect
sections.body: Review site placement, replication source, and prerequisite results; install and restart.

sections.heading: Inspect both controllers and replication
sections.body:
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * |
  Select-Object HostName, IPv4Address, IsGlobalCatalog
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl SBD-DC02

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: Both hostnames appear with the intended addresses and global catalog roles. After initial convergence, replication checks show successful recent attempts and no unresolved replication failures. Inspect errors rather than assuming the restart completed replication.

sections.heading: Avoid this mistake
sections.body: Choosing Add a new forest creates a different directory. For this chapter, DC02 joins the domain established by DC01.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record both controllers, replication status and collection time, plus any failures or follow-up actions.

quizzes.question: A damaging directory change reaches both controllers. What does that illustrate?
answers: DC02 should never replicate
Two controllers guarantee recovery
Replication and historical recovery are different capabilities
quizzes.explanation: Both controllers can hold the same unwanted change. Recovery requires protected backups and an appropriate, tested recovery procedure.

lessons.title: Ask the domain to prove it works
lessons.summary: Check each controller's health, replication in both directions, the roles each holds, and its host firewall.

sections.heading: Understand the why
sections.body: A service can be running while the domain is unhealthy. Test each controller by name so every result tells you which controller you checked. Capture actual results and failures in your evidence record.

sections.heading: What crosses the network?
sections.body: The ports a domain member needs to reach its domain controllers.

sections.heading: Every conversation crosses the core
sections.body: Domain members sit on other segments, so each conversation in this table crosses the core, which allows it only because a rule says so. Inside the Network shows each one crossing the core switch.

sections.heading: Sign-in is only the start
sections.body: Kerberos proves who is signing in. After that, the member reads the directory over LDAP, pulls Group Policy and scripts from SYSVOL over SMB, and uses RPC for NetLogon. Time matters too: Kerberos rejects clocks that drift too far apart.

sections.heading: Remember
sections.body: Allowing Kerberos isn't enough. Applying Group Policy and reading SYSVOL also need LDAP, SMB, and RPC. In the Inside the Network design, rules F02, F03, and F09 permit this profile for domain members, with LDAP signing and channel binding required, and rule A01 limits administration to the Tier 0 host. Name resolution (F01) and credentialed scanning (F15) have their own rules; everything else is denied.

sections.heading: Test each controller
sections.body: In an elevated PowerShell window on either controller, run DCDiag against SBD-DC01 and then SBD-DC02. Its default tests cover connectivity, advertising, replication, SYSVOL, services, and role holders. Read each test's result, not just the last line.

sections.heading: Check replication both ways
sections.body: Run the replication summary, then list each controller's inbound partners. Expect recent successful attempts from DC01 to DC02 and from DC02 to DC01, with no failures. If an error appears right after promotion, wait a few minutes and run the checks again; record any error that persists.

sections.heading: Confirm both controllers' roles
sections.body: List both controllers with their global catalog status, then the operations master (FSMO) role holders; in this build SBD-DC01 holds all five. Confirm SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on SBD-DC02 as well. If they are not, its first SYSVOL replication has not finished.

sections.heading: Confirm the second layer
sections.body: On each controller, confirm the network profile is DomainAuthenticated and that the effective firewall policy is on for the Domain, Private, and Public profiles and blocks unsolicited inbound connections. A controller that reports the Public or Private profile is applying a different rule set than the domain expects; find out why before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Read-only domain health checks
sections.body:
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC01
dcdiag /s:SBD-DC02
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl *
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object HostName, IsGlobalCatalog
netdom query fsmo
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON -CimSession SBD-DC02
Get-NetConnectionProfile | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, NetworkCategory
Get-NetFirewallProfile -PolicyStore ActiveStore |
  Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: Each controller passes its DCDiag tests, or every failure has a recorded cause. Replication shows recent successful attempts in both directions and no failures. Both controllers are global catalogs, SBD-DC01 holds the five operations master roles, SYSVOL and NETLOGON are shared on both, and each controller reports the DomainAuthenticated profile with every firewall profile on and inbound blocked by default. Save output with host, time, and interpretation; a command that ran is not a pass.

sections.heading: Avoid this mistake
sections.body: A successful ping proves only that an address answers. It doesn't show that the directory replicates, that SYSVOL is shared, or that a controller can authenticate anyone.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: For each controller, record the DCDiag results, replication status in both directions, the roles it holds, its network profile and firewall state, the test time, and what the results establish.

quizzes.question: repadmin /replsummary reports no failures. What does that establish?
answers: The most recent replication attempts between the controllers succeeded
Every authentication control is satisfied
The system is authorized to operate
quizzes.explanation: The summary describes the latest attempts at that moment. Authentication requirements, recovery, and authorization need their own evidence and decisions.

lessons.title: Leave a build someone else can understand
lessons.summary: Assemble your configuration record, test evidence, and remaining work.

sections.heading: Understand the why
sections.body: The useful deliverable is a build you can explain and check again. Your evidence record connects each action with an observed result and identifies what remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Describe the final state
sections.body: Record the domain, both controllers, their segment and gateway, site placement, and actual role holders. Preserve the distinction between the intended design and observed configuration.

sections.heading: Keep a small evidence set
sections.body: Store your environment outputs locally with descriptive filenames and collection times. In this companion, write a short summary and the file references; the form does not upload or collect your screenshots, server output, or credentials.

sections.heading: Plan the next check
sections.body: List remaining hardening, auditing, backup, recovery, and client-validation work. Assign an owner or next action. Revisit checks after relevant configuration changes. Export the evidence record before moving devices.

sections.heading: Record the current role holders
sections.body:
Get-ADDomain |
  Select-Object DNSRoot, PDCEmulator, RIDMaster, InfrastructureMaster
Get-ADForest |
  Select-Object RootDomain, SchemaMaster, DomainNamingMaster

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: The record identifies the actual role holders and links configuration decisions to dated test results. Open issues remain visible. Lesson completion records learning activity; it is not a system authorization decision.

sections.heading: Avoid this mistake
sections.body: A diagram becoming complete does not establish that your VM passed a check. The model tells the lesson story; your observations establish what happened in your environment.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Summarize the final state, reference your evidence files, and list remaining work with a next action or review trigger.

quizzes.question: Which event is a useful reason to revisit the evidence?
answers: Only the anniversary of the video
A relevant configuration change or new finding
Finishing the animation
quizzes.explanation: Changes and findings can affect prior conclusions. A monitoring plan defines when and how to reassess the relevant security state.

courses.title: Configure DNS and time
courses.subtitle: Service discovery, zones, records, domain time & troubleshooting
courses.description: Learn how DNS lets every domain member find its domain controllers, then build dependable internal name resolution and time on DC01 and DC02: set each controller's DNS order, configure forward and reverse zones, manage service records, make the PDC emulator the domain's time source, and prove both in the air-gapped training network.

materials.title: Configure DNS and time · Interactive guide
materials.description: Service discovery, zones, records, domain time & troubleshooting

materials.title: Configure DNS and time · Training materials (ZIP)
materials.description: Workbook (PDF and Word), checklist, and verification commands.

lessons.title: Map names to the network
lessons.summary: Domain Name System (DNS) turns names into addresses, and for Active Directory it does one more job: it tells every domain member where its domain controllers are. Start from the working directory build, learn what DNS answers and what it doesn't, set each controller's DNS client order, and record which server owns each name and how a client finds it.
objectives: Explain how DNS lets a domain member find a domain controller, and what a DNS answer does not prove.
Set each domain controller's DNS client order and point domain members only at internal DNS.
Inventory the existing sbd.test and _msdcs zones without creating duplicates.
Document the forwarding and recursion decision for an air-gapped network.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Start with what DNS answers. An A record maps a host name to an IPv4 address (AAAA maps to IPv6), so SBD-DC01.sbd.test resolves to 10.0.10.10. Service (SRV) records advertise which servers offer a service: a domain member asks for _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test, resolves a listed controller's name, contacts it, and only then authenticates. DNS never checks a password, and it works on an isolated network with no internet access.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Record the domain, each subnet, both DNS addresses, and the owner of each service name. Keep host records and service aliases distinguishable.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: On each domain controller, confirm the DNS Server service is installed and running; an address typed into a network adapter installs nothing. Then open DNS Manager and review the sbd.test and _msdcs.sbd.test zones that promotion created, without creating duplicates. The DNS delegation warning from course 1.1's promotion is expected: no parent zone exists above the isolated .test namespace, so no action is needed.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Set each controller's DNS client order. Promotion pointed SBD-DC01 at itself (the loopback address, 127.0.0.1) while it was the only controller, and SBD-DC02 pointed at SBD-DC01 so it could find the domain. Run the replication summary first; once replication succeeds in both directions, list the partner controller first and the loopback address second on each, and never an outside resolver. Domain members list both controllers; a public resolver is not an alternate for this environment.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Confirm the network's service-path register permits DNS: every networked system to both domain controllers on TCP and UDP 53 (rule F01 in Inside the Network). A member has to find a controller before any Kerberos, LDAP, or Group Policy traffic can start.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Decide whether any separate internal namespace needs a conditional forwarder. With no recursive dependencies, document a no-recursion design; do not add internet forwarders or delete every root hint as a shortcut.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02 { Get-WindowsFeature DNS; Get-Service DNS }
repadmin /replsummary
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 -CimSession SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02
# After replication succeeds both ways (adapter name varies):
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -CimSession SBD-DC01 -InterfaceAlias Ethernet `
  -ServerAddresses 10.0.10.11,127.0.0.1
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -CimSession SBD-DC02 -InterfaceAlias Ethernet `
  -ServerAddresses 10.0.10.10,127.0.0.1
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 -CimSession SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName SBD-DC01

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both controllers run the DNS Server service and, once replication succeeds both ways, list their partner first and the loopback address second. Members list both controllers only; the AD zones, the recursion decision, and the register rows that permit DNS are recorded.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Save the address/name worksheet, each controller's DNS client order and the reason for it, and the initial zone inventory before changing anything else.

quizzes.question: Which DNS servers should a domain member use in this lab?
answers: The internal DNS servers that resolve sbd.test
A public resolver whenever the first DC is unavailable
The offline Root CA
quizzes.explanation: AD clients need the internal namespace and its service records. Internet reachability would not replace that requirement.

quizzes.question: Promotion already created the sbd.test and _msdcs zones. What should you do?
answers: Delete them and start from a clean zone list
Review and record them without creating duplicate zones
Create a second sbd.test zone for DC02
quizzes.explanation: Promotion builds the zones Active Directory needs. Duplicating or recreating them breaks the record you are trying to verify.

quizzes.question: Why does this design document a no-recursion decision instead of adding internet forwarders?
answers: Forwarders are always a security violation
Root hints make zones replicate faster
The network has no recursive dependencies, so the decision is recorded deliberately
quizzes.explanation: In an air-gapped lab there is nothing to forward to. Writing the decision down keeps the design intentional rather than accidental.

quizzes.question: Why did SBD-DC02 point to SBD-DC01 for DNS while it was promoted?
answers: Its own DNS service didn't exist yet, and SBD-DC01 held the records that locate the domain
A domain controller can never use its own DNS service
Promotion needs an internet resolver
quizzes.explanation: A new controller finds the existing domain through DNS. Until replication has given its own DNS service a current copy of the zones, it relies on a controller that already has one.

quizzes.question: You can reach 10.0.10.10, but a member still can't find a domain controller for sbd.test. What do you inspect first?
answers: The Kerberos ticket lifetime
The member's DNS server list and the SRV records on the servers it uses
The forest functional level
quizzes.explanation: Reaching an address isn't discovery. Check that the member asks the internal DNS servers and that they hold the domain controller locator records.

recap: DNS finds domain controllers through SRV records; it never checks a password.
Each controller lists its partner, then itself; members list both controllers only.
The AD zones are inventoried, not recreated, and the delegation warning is expected.
The forwarding and recursion decision is written down first.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 turns this plan into AD-integrated forward and reverse zones.

lessons.title: Configure forward and reverse zones
lessons.summary: A zone holds the records for one part of the namespace. Forward lookup answers where a name lives. Reverse lookup answers which name is assigned to an address. AD integration lets the directory replicate zone data between the selected DNS servers.
objectives: Confirm sbd.test is AD-integrated with the intended replication scope.
Create a secure, AD-integrated reverse zone for 10.0.10.0/24.
Explain how zone data moves between the two DNS hosts.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: In DNS Manager, inspect sbd.test Properties. Confirm that it is AD-integrated and choose the domain or forest replication scope that matches the DNS servers intended to host it. Domain-wide zones live in the DomainDnsZones partition and forest-wide zones in ForestDnsZones, the partitions you saw in course 1.1's replication and DCDiag output.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Use secure dynamic updates for the AD-integrated zone. Review delegation and permissions before broadening who can change records.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Under Reverse Lookup Zones, create an IPv4 primary AD-integrated zone for network ID 10.0.10 if an equivalent zone does not already exist. Select the approved replication scope and secure updates.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Review zone-transfer settings. AD replication between these DCs does not require enabling transfers to arbitrary DNS servers; restrict any separately required secondary-server transfers explicitly.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName SBD-DC01 |
  Select-Object ZoneName, ZoneType, IsDsIntegrated, DynamicUpdate, ReplicationScope
Get-DnsServerZone -ComputerName SBD-DC02

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The intended forward and reverse zones appear on both DNS hosts after replication. The reverse zone for this /24 is 10.0.10.in-addr.arpa.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Capture the zone type, update policy, replication scope, and transfer policy for each zone.

Microsoft · Manage DNS zones

Microsoft · Active Directory-integrated DNS zones

quizzes.question: How does an AD-integrated zone reach the other DNS-enabled domain controller in its replication scope?
answers: An unrestricted zone transfer to every client
Active Directory replication
A manual copy of the DNS cache
quizzes.explanation: AD-integrated zone data follows directory replication. A conventional secondary zone uses a different transfer mechanism.

quizzes.question: What is the reverse lookup zone for the 10.0.10.0/24 network?
answers: 10.0.10.in-addr.arpa
sbd.test.reverse
quizzes.explanation: IPv4 reverse zones place the reversed network octets under in-addr.arpa, so this /24 becomes 10.0.10.in-addr.arpa.

quizzes.question: Why choose secure dynamic updates for the AD-integrated zone?
answers: It makes lookups return faster
It removes the need for a reverse zone
Only authenticated computers can register or change their records
quizzes.explanation: Secure updates tie record changes to directory authentication, which keeps the zone’s contents accountable.

recap: Forward and reverse zones are AD-integrated with a deliberate replication scope.
Dynamic updates are secure-only.
Zone transfers stay restricted; directory replication moves the data.

lessons.title: Create and maintain service records
lessons.summary: Build a small, intentional record set. A host record identifies a machine; an alias provides a stable service name without making that alias a separate server.
objectives: Distinguish host records (A and PTR) from service aliases (CNAME).
Create a host record with its PTR and a service alias that match the plan.
Maintain records with recorded ownership, lifetimes, and reasons.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Review the DC A and PTR records first. Correct mismatches through the owning host and DNS administration process rather than blindly adding another record with the same name.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Choose one approved service host from your address plan. In sbd.test, use New Host (A or AAAA), enter its actual name and address, and select the associated PTR option when the reverse zone is ready.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: For a service alias, use New Alias (CNAME) and select the intended fully qualified host. For the later PKI course, reserve pki.sbd.test for the approved internal publication host; do not point it at the offline root.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Set the record lifetime to the operational plan, record static ownership, and remove only records confirmed obsolete. An alias cannot coexist with other record types at the same name.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-DnsServerResourceRecord -ComputerName SBD-DC01 -ZoneName sbd.test
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Type A -Server 10.0.10.10
Resolve-DnsName 10.0.10.10 -Type PTR -Server 10.0.10.10

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Forward and reverse responses agree with the address plan. Each alias reaches the intended host; creating a DNS name alone does not configure its service.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep a record table with owner, type, target, time to live, and reason for the change.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Manage DNS resource records
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/dns/manage-resource-records

quizzes.question: What does creating pki.sbd.test as an alias accomplish?
answers: It publishes every certificate automatically
It connects the offline root to the network
It points a service name at the selected host
quizzes.explanation: DNS supplies name resolution. The publication service, files, access, and certificate URLs still need configuration.

quizzes.question: A CNAME already exists at a name. What else can live at that same name?
answers: Any A record
No other record types
A second CNAME
quizzes.explanation: An alias cannot coexist with other record types at the same name — one reason service aliases are planned deliberately.

quizzes.question: Forward and reverse answers disagree for a domain controller. What is the right fix?
answers: Correct it through the owning host and the DNS administration process
Add another record with the same name
Delete the reverse zone
quizzes.explanation: Mismatches get fixed at the owner, not papered over with duplicates that make troubleshooting harder.

recap: Host records identify machines; aliases provide stable service names.
pki.sbd.test is reserved for the internal publication host, never the offline root.
Every record carries an owner, a lifetime, and a reason.

lessons.title: Prove resolution and directory discovery
lessons.summary: Test each server explicitly before testing client fallback. A successful cached answer does not prove that both DNS servers hold the right records, and a correct DNS answer proves neither a successful sign-in nor access to a protected resource.
objectives: Query each DNS server explicitly instead of trusting cached answers.
Verify the locator (SRV) records that let clients discover domain controllers.
Run a controlled failover test and record the result.
Optionally capture a locator query and compare it with the model's packet card.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: From a domain client or either controller, query each DNS server by address for both controllers' host records, so each result tells you which server answered. Expect SBD-DC01.sbd.test at 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02.sbd.test at 10.0.10.11 from both servers.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Query the domain controller locator service (SRV) records against both servers. These records let a client discover domain controllers; an ordinary host lookup does not prove discovery works, and a locator answer does not by itself prove that every listed controller is reachable.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Run the DNS diagnostics against every domain controller, then the replication summary. Classify root-hint, forwarder, and delegation findings against the documented isolated design instead of treating them as faults, and investigate everything else.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: During an approved lab test, make one DNS server unavailable to the test client and verify resolution through the other. Restore connectivity and repeat for the opposite server. Do not interrupt shared production services for this exercise.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Optional: see the locator query on the wire. On SBD-DC02, in an elevated PowerShell window, capture port 53 with Packet Monitor (pktmon), which is built into Windows Server, while you query SBD-DC01, so the request crosses the network. Expect a query from 10.0.10.11 to 10.0.10.10 on UDP port 53 and an answer naming both controllers on port 389. Read the text file, or open the .pcapng file in a packet analyzer such as Wireshark, and keep the capture with your evidence; it holds only the traffic the filter allowed.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
foreach ($server in '10.0.10.10','10.0.10.11') {
  Write-Output "DNS server: $server"
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC01.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC02.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test' -Type SRV -Server $server
}
dcdiag /test:DNS /e /v
repadmin /replsummary
# Optional, on SBD-DC02: capture the locator query
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence -Force
pktmon filter remove
pktmon filter add DNS -p 53
pktmon start --capture --comp nics --pkt-size 0 --file-name C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl
Resolve-DnsName '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test' -Type SRV -Server 10.0.10.10
pktmon stop
pktmon etl2txt C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl --out C:\Evidence\dc-locator.txt
pktmon etl2pcap C:\Evidence\dc-locator.etl --out C:\Evidence\dc-locator.pcapng
pktmon filter remove

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both DNS servers return both controllers' host records and the domain controller locator records, the DCDiag DNS findings are explained, replication is healthy, and the client still resolves internal names when either resolver is unavailable. If you ran the capture, it shows the query from 10.0.10.11 and the answer from 10.0.10.10.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep paired lookup results with the server queried, the DCDiag and replication output, the failover test record with start, restore, and final verification times, any capture file, and a short statement of what the results do and don't establish: DNS helps users find the identity service, but a correct answer proves nothing about authentication.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Locating domain controllers
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/dc-locator-changes

Microsoft · Resolve-DnsName
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname

Microsoft · Dcdiag
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/dcdiag

Microsoft · Packet Monitor (pktmon)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/pktmon

quizzes.question: Why query each DNS server directly?
answers: To distinguish a healthy pair from a single working resolver or cached answer
To permanently bypass the client's DNS configuration
To generate a certificate request
quizzes.explanation: Explicit server queries expose differences between resolvers before client caching and fallback obscure the result.

quizzes.question: Which record type lets a client discover domain controllers?
answers: PTR records in the reverse zone
CNAME aliases such as pki.sbd.test
SRV records such as _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test
quizzes.explanation: Service (SRV) records advertise the directory service. An ordinary host lookup does not prove discovery works.

quizzes.question: During the failover exercise, what belongs in the evidence record?
answers: Only a screenshot of one successful lookup
Start, restore, and final verification times with the paired lookup results
The DNS service account password
quizzes.explanation: A dated failover record shows redundancy was proven, not assumed — and secrets never belong in evidence.

quizzes.question: What does a successful domain controller locator query establish?
answers: Every authentication control is satisfied
The queried server returned the requested service records
The system is authorized to operate
quizzes.explanation: The query demonstrates one DNS response. Reachability, authentication, control effectiveness, and authorization need their own evidence and decisions.

quizzes.question: A ping to 10.0.10.10 succeeds. What has it proved?
answers: That DNS service discovery works
That sign-in will succeed
Only that the address answered
quizzes.explanation: Ping confirms limited IP reachability. It says nothing about service discovery, directory replication, or authentication.

recap: Both resolvers answer the host and SRV queries correctly.
dcdiag and repadmin confirm DNS and replication health, with isolated-design findings explained.
The failover test is documented with times, not just a passing screenshot.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 gives the domain a trustworthy clock, the other dependency every sign-in relies on.

lessons.title: Make SBD-DC01 the domain's time source
lessons.summary: Kerberos tolerates minutes of skew, not more, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Make the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01, the domain's authoritative time source and let the domain hierarchy carry its time to everything else.
objectives: Configure SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, as the domain's reliable time source.
Keep every other system on the domain hierarchy, with nothing overriding it.
Document how DC01's clock is set and checked, and the drift threshold the model calls for.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Confirm which domain controller holds the PDC emulator role — SBD-DC01 in this sample. The PDC emulator of the forest root domain sits at the top of the Windows Time hierarchy, so it is the one system you configure; everything else follows it.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: On SBD-DC01, mark Windows Time as a reliable time source with no external peer, so it serves time from its own clock. In an air-gapped network that clock is the reference by declaration: record how it is set and checked — for example, compared on a schedule against an approved reference and corrected by an administrator, with each correction recorded — and the drift threshold you will hold it to.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for both domain controller virtual machines, so the host clock cannot silently override the PDC emulator. SBD-DC02 syncs from the PDC emulator, every other domain member keeps the default domain-hierarchy sync from the domain controllers, and the domain-joined Linux servers in later courses point chrony or ntpd at both domain controllers.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Confirm the network's service-path register permits time — every member to both domain controllers on UDP 123 — and write the time design into the build record: course 1.3's hardening Group Policy objects (GPOs) must leave it intact, and if a Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) value disagrees with it, that course's deviation record is where the decision lives.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Verify the chain end to end: SBD-DC01 serving as the reliable source, SBD-DC02 and a member server sourcing from a domain controller, and offsets within your recorded threshold.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator   # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# On SBD-DC01 (the PDC emulator): serve time from its own clock as the reliable source
w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update
Restart-Service w32time
w32tm /query /source   # on SBD-DC01: Local CMOS Clock
# On SBD-DC02 and a member server:
w32tm /query /source   # expected: a domain controller
w32tm /query /status
w32tm /stripchart /computer:SBD-DC01.sbd.test /samples:3 /dataonly

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: SBD-DC01 reports itself as the reliable source (Local CMOS Clock), SBD-DC02 and the member server report a domain controller, host time synchronization is off for both domain controllers, and measured offsets sit inside the documented threshold.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the time design decisions (how DC01's clock is set and checked, and the drift threshold), the source and status output from both controllers and the member, the stripchart offsets, the hypervisor setting for both domain controller VMs, and the register rows that permit time: every member to the domain controllers.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Windows Time service
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/windows-time-service/windows-time-service-top

Microsoft · Windows Time service tools and settings
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/windows-time-service/windows-time-service-tools-and-settings

quizzes.question: Which system is the domain's authoritative time source in this design?
answers: Every domain member individually
SBD-DC01, the domain controller holding the PDC emulator role
The offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The PDC emulator of the forest root domain is the top of the Windows Time hierarchy. Marking it reliable makes it the source everything else follows.

quizzes.question: What does the air gap change about time design?
answers: Nothing — pool.ntp.org still works
Kerberos stops needing accurate time
There is no internet source, so DC01's clock is the reference by declaration and how it is checked is a documented decision
quizzes.explanation: With no external source, accuracy is whatever the lab declares and monitors — which is why the time-stamp controls (AU-8, SC-45) land on the PDC emulator.

quizzes.question: Why does time matter to authentication at all?
answers: Kerberos rejects tickets outside its allowed clock skew, so drifting clocks become sign-in failures
DNS records expire hourly
Passwords change with the clock
quizzes.explanation: Kerberos builds replay protection on timestamps. Skew beyond the tolerance breaks authentication before anything looks wrong.

quizzes.question: Why turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for the domain controller virtual machines?
answers: It saves processor time
Windows Time will not start otherwise
The host clock would silently override the PDC emulator and fight the domain hierarchy
quizzes.explanation: A virtual machine that takes time from its host has two masters. Turning host sync off leaves the domain hierarchy, rooted at the PDC emulator, as the only authority.

quizzes.question: Where does a domain workstation get its time in this design?
answers: From SBD-DC01 only, set by hand on each machine
From a domain controller over UDP 123, following the domain hierarchy
From the core router
quizzes.explanation: Windows Time follows the domain hierarchy: members sync from a domain controller, the other domain controller from the PDC emulator, and the PDC emulator from its own clock. That is why the register permits UDP 123 from every VLAN to the domain controllers.

recap: SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, is the declared source; how its clock is checked is written down.
The hypervisor no longer overrides domain controller time; the hierarchy carries it everywhere.
Offsets are measured and inside the threshold, not assumed.
lessons.next: The final lesson practices finding and documenting a DNS or time fault.

lessons.title: Find the fault and record the fix
lessons.summary: Troubleshoot one layer at a time: client settings, server reachability, authoritative data, replication, and finally the application that uses the name.
objectives: Isolate a DNS failure one layer at a time.
Distinguish a missing name (NXDOMAIN) from timeouts and service failures.
Record the cause, the fix, and the rollback — not just a passing result.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.1, the DC01 + DC02 identity build, with both domain controllers healthy. Both were promoted with the DNS server option selected, and SBD-DC02 still uses SBD-DC01 for DNS.

Use an isolated Windows Server practice environment and an account delegated to manage DNS.

Continue the existing sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 is 10.0.10.10 and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11 on 10.0.10.0/24.

The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The addresses and names below continue the training example. Match every change to your own address plan. This network has no internet DNS or time dependency: names resolve on the domain controllers, and time comes from the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: For a failing lookup, record the exact name, record type, client, resolver, timestamp, and error. Compare the fully qualified name with any short-name search behavior.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Query both servers directly. If they disagree, inspect zone scope and replication. If both are correct but the client is not, inspect client DNS settings and cached data.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Distinguish a missing name (NXDOMAIN) from a timeout or service failure. Fix the owning configuration first, then use Clear-DnsClientCache on the test client if stale cache remains relevant.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Repeat the original test and the redundancy checks. Record what changed and the rollback method. Review aging/scavenging separately against DHCP, static records, and backup practices before enabling automatic deletion.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4
Get-DnsClientCache
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.10
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test -Server 10.0.10.11

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The original failure is reproducibly resolved, both resolvers agree, and the change record explains the cause rather than only showing a passing screenshot.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Complete the DNS checklist and retain the before/after lookup results with the configuration owner.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Manage DNS resource records
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/dns/manage-resource-records

Microsoft · Resolve-DnsName
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname

quizzes.question: Both DNS servers return the correct address, but one client keeps using the old address. What should you inspect next?
answers: The Root CA private key
The client resolver configuration and cache
Every zone's transfer policy at once
quizzes.explanation: Narrow the investigation to the failing client before changing otherwise consistent authoritative data.

quizzes.question: A lookup returns NXDOMAIN from both servers. What does that tell you?
answers: The name does not exist in the authoritative data
The DNS service is stopped
The client cache is corrupted
quizzes.explanation: NXDOMAIN is an authoritative answer that the name is missing — a different problem from a timeout or an unreachable service.

quizzes.question: When is Clear-DnsClientCache the right step?
answers: As the first step for every DNS problem
After the owning configuration is fixed, when stale cached data remains relevant
Instead of checking the authoritative servers
quizzes.explanation: Clearing the cache hides symptoms if the authoritative data is still wrong. Fix the owner first, then clear what is stale.

recap: Troubleshoot client settings, reachability, authoritative data, replication, then the application.
NXDOMAIN, timeouts, and service failures point at different owners.
The change record explains the cause and the rollback.

lessons.title: Design and build the OU structure
lessons.summary: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.
objectives: Design an OU structure around delegation and Group Policy targeting.
Create protected OUs and redirect the default Computers and Users containers.
Explain why the built-in Domain Controllers OU stays untouched.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete the identity build and DNS courses with replication and name resolution verified on both controllers.

Use the isolated Windows Server environment and an account approved for organizational unit and Group Policy administration.

Have an approved connected system and removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded hardening content into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course designs the organizational unit (OU) structure, applies the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy package, and verifies the result with Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) scans. Paths, versions, and session locations below are examples — adapt them to your tooling. Expect STIG settings to change behavior: that is the point, and the reason everything is scanned and recorded.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Design the structure by administration: a top-level SBD OU containing Servers, Workstations, Users, Groups, and an Admin OU for privileged accounts. The built-in Domain Controllers OU stays where it is and keeps its name.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create the planned OUs with accidental-deletion protection enabled. Record each OU's purpose and who will administer its contents; an OU with no delegation or policy purpose is clutter.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Redirect the default Computers and Users containers to managed OUs with redircmp and redirusr. Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so anything landing there would get only domain-level policy, never the OU-linked hardening.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Keep privileged accounts and systems separate: the Admin OU holds the identities that administer domain controllers. The issuing CA from course 1.4 joins the Servers OU for now; course 1.5 gives Tier 0 servers their own OU. Do not nest deeper than the delegation plan requires.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object ComputersContainer, UsersContainer
(Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity 'OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Properties ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion).ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The planned OUs exist with deletion protection, the default container redirects point at managed OUs, and each OU has a recorded purpose and administrator.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the OU design sheet: each OU's distinguished name, purpose, delegated administrator, and the redirect commands with their output.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · New-ADOrganizationalUnit
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/new-adorganizationalunit

Microsoft · Redirect the Users and Computers containers
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/active-directory/redirect-users-computers-containers

quizzes.question: What should drive the shape of the OU structure?
answers: Group Policy targeting and delegated administration
The company org chart
Alphabetical order of departments
quizzes.explanation: OUs are an administrative tool. Policy and delegation boundaries define them; reporting lines belong in HR systems.

quizzes.question: Why redirect the default Computers container?
answers: It makes domain join faster
Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so new machines would miss the OU-linked hardening
It is required before DNS works
quizzes.explanation: Redirection sends newly joined machines into an OU where policy applies from their first start.

quizzes.question: Where do the two domain controllers live after this lesson?
answers: In the new Servers OU
In the built-in Domain Controllers OU, unchanged
In the Users container
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers stay in their built-in OU — it is where the DC hardening policies link in lesson 4.

recap: OUs follow administration, not the org chart.
The default containers are redirected so nothing joins unmanaged.
The Domain Controllers OU remains the link point for DC policies.

lessons.title: Stage the tooling across the air gap
lessons.summary: The hardening content is downloaded artifacts: the DISA Group Policy object (GPO) package, the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC), and STIG Viewer. They cross the boundary the way everything does here — reviewed, hashed, and carried on approved removable media.
objectives: Identify the DISA artifacts the hardening work needs.
Move downloaded tooling across the air gap with hash verification.
Record versions so scans stay comparable over time.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete the identity build and DNS courses with replication and name resolution verified on both controllers.

Use the isolated Windows Server environment and an account approved for organizational unit and Group Policy administration.

Have an approved connected system and removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded hardening content into the lab.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course designs the organizational unit (OU) structure, applies the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy package, and verifies the result with Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) scans. Paths, versions, and session locations below are examples — adapt them to your tooling. Expect STIG settings to change behavior: that is the point, and the reason everything is scanned and recorded.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: On an approved connected system, download the current DISA GPO package and the SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer) from DISA's public site. Note each file's version and the quarterly release it belongs to.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Record a SHA-256 hash for every file on the connected side, then transfer the set with the approved removable-media procedure. No live link to the lab is created for convenience.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: In the lab, recalculate and compare every hash before opening anything. A mismatch stops the work, exactly as it would in the PKI signing ceremony.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Install SCC and STIG Viewer on an administrative host and stage the GPO package where the import lesson can reach it. Record tool versions; scan results are only comparable when the benchmark and tool versions are known.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA | Select-Object Name, Length

lessons.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
lessons.summary: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.
objectives: Explain why the root stays offline while the issuing CA handles enrollment.
Record the CA identities, cryptography, lifetimes, and CRL periods before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
Plan AIA and CDP publication locations that clients can reach inside the air gap.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.3 (identity, DNS and time, and the hardened baseline); verify domain health and internal name resolution.

Prepare separate Windows Server hosts: SBD-ROOTCA01 in a disconnected workgroup, SBD-SUBCA01 joined to sbd.test, and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as a hardened member server at 10.0.30.30 in the Servers OU (course 1.5 moves it, with the issuing CA, to a Tier 0 Servers OU).

Approve the CA names, cryptography, validity periods, publication URLs, administration, backups, and removable-media procedure before installation; confirm the network's service-path register permits HTTP to pki.sbd.test.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the whole PKI: a standalone offline Root CA, an enterprise subordinate/issuing CA, the pki.sbd.test publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01, and template administration on its own seat. The root stays disconnected; approved removable media carries requests and public artifacts. Publication stays plain HTTP by design — clients must be able to fetch revocation data before they can validate any certificate.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Draw the hierarchy: offline standalone root → enterprise issuing CA → approved server/client certificates. There is no network connection to the root.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Record final host and CA names, key provider, algorithm, key sizes, hashes, validity periods, renewal owners, and recovery arrangements. Start from this lab's example values in the next step and change any that your own policy requires: they are examples, not universal requirements.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Example values for this lab: the root CA uses an RSA 4096 key with SHA-256 and a 20-year certificate, and publishes a base CRL every 26 weeks with an overlap period and no delta CRL, refreshed at each offline ceremony. The issuing CA uses RSA 4096 (3072 at minimum) with SHA-256 and a 10-year certificate, a weekly base CRL, and a daily delta CRL. End-entity certificates last one to two years. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 rates RSA 2048 at 112 bits of security, which it accepts for new signatures only through 2030, so a CA that will still be signing after 2030 uses at least 3072 bits (128 bits of security); the newest Windows Server release requires at least 2,048-bit RSA for TLS server authentication.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Know where each value is set. You choose the key, the hash, and the root's 20-year validity in the AD CS Configuration wizard. Each CA's CAPolicy.inf sets its CRL periods (CRLPeriod, CRLPeriodUnits, CRLDeltaPeriod, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits), which certutil -setreg can change later. The issuing CA's 10-year lifetime is set on the root (CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits) before the signing ceremony, because a subordinate CA's lifetime comes from the CA that signs it.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Plan a stable internal publication name such as pki.sbd.test. The Authority Information Access (AIA) location supplies issuer certificates; the CRL Distribution Point (CDP) supplies certificate revocation lists.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: Choose the publication host, paths, access rules, and refresh schedule before issuing certificates. Clients inside this air-gapped network must reach those locations without relying on the public internet.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Run on the future issuing CA, not the offline root.
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The written plan separates trust, issuance, publication, and administration. It identifies who renews CRLs before they expire, and every key size, hash, lifetime, and CRL period has a recorded value and the setting that applies it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the approved hierarchy, the cryptography and lifetime table with the setting that applies each value, and a worksheet mapping every certificate/CRL URL to its actual publisher and file.

answers: The offline root for every request

quizzes.explanation: The issuing CA handles end-entity enrollment while the offline root signs the approved subordinate CA certificate.

quizzes.question: What do the AIA and CDP locations supply?
answers: Private keys for backup
DNS zone transfers
Issuer certificates and certificate revocation lists
quizzes.explanation: Authority Information Access serves issuer certificates; CRL Distribution Points serve revocation lists. Clients must be able to reach both.

quizzes.question: Why is pki.sbd.test planned before any CA is installed?
answers: Issued certificates embed these URLs, so the publication name must be stable first
The root cannot be installed without it
DNS requires a CNAME before zones replicate
quizzes.explanation: Certificates keep the extensions they were issued with. A stable publication name avoids reissuing everything later.

quizzes.question: In this lab, where is the issuing CA's 10-year certificate lifetime set?
answers: In the issuing CA's own CAPolicy.inf
On the offline root, with CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits, before the signing ceremony
In the certificate template for web servers
quizzes.explanation: A subordinate CA's lifetime is set by the CA that signs it. The root's issued-certificate validity settings decide how long the issuing CA's certificate lasts, so they are set and verified before the ceremony.

recap: Trust, issuance, publication, and administration are separated in writing.
Cryptography, names, lifetimes, and CRL periods are approved before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
CRL renewal has a named owner and a date.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the whole PKI: a standalone offline Root CA, an enterprise subordinate/issuing CA, the pki.sbd.test publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01, and template administration on its own seat. The root stays disconnected; approved removable media carries requests and public artifacts. Publication stays plain HTTP by design — clients must be able to fetch revocation data before they can validate any certificate.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Verify SBD-ROOTCA01 is in a workgroup with no active network path. Prepare approved installation media, protected administration, correct time, and backup storage.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Place the reviewed CAPolicy.inf in %SystemRoot% before configuration. Tailor it to the root role: in this lab it sets CRLPeriod=Weeks and CRLPeriodUnits=26, and CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=0 so the root publishes no delta CRL. A self-signed root's own CDP/AIA choices differ from the extensions the root places into issued subordinate certificates.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Install the Certification Authority role with management tools. In the AD CS Configuration wizard choose Standalone CA, Root CA, and a new private key, then apply the approved provider, cryptography (RSA 4096 with SHA-256 in this lab), CA name, validity (20 years), database, and log settings.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Before signing anything, configure the root's issued-certificate AIA/CDP settings, the subordinate validity policy (CA\ValidityPeriod Years and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits 10 in this lab), and the base-CRL schedule (26 weeks with an overlap period, and no delta CRL). Hold requests for explicit approval. Produce and inspect a current root CRL, then capture a protected CA backup.

sections.body: Duplicate the Web Server template as SBD Server Authentication for the business services in course 1.9: enrollment permission for the server administrators, no autoenrollment, and exportable keys only if the recovery plan explicitly says so.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Record each template's version, settings, and justification through the lesson-3 change process before publishing.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Publish exactly these two templates on the issuing CA and remove any default template the plan does not call for — an unpublished template cannot be mis-enrolled.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
certutil -CATemplates -config 'SBD-SUBCA01\SBD Issuing CA'
certutil -template 'SBDComputerAuthentication' | Select-String 'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag','msPKI-Minimal-Key-Size'

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The CA publishes exactly the two planned templates, each shows the approved key size and permissions, and both carry a completed change record.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep each template's configuration export, its change record, and the CA's published-template listing.

quizzes.question: Why duplicate the built-in templates instead of editing them?
answers: Built-ins cannot be published at all
Duplication preserves the originals and gives your version its own name, version, and record
Duplicates issue faster
quizzes.explanation: Working on a named copy keeps the baseline intact and makes your settings — and their history — unmistakably yours.

quizzes.question: What floor applies to the template key sizes on this network?
answers: 512 bits for speed
1,024 bits
2,048-bit RSA at minimum — the newest Windows Server release enforces it for TLS server authentication
quizzes.explanation: The newest Windows Server release requires at least 2,048-bit RSA keys for TLS server authentication, so a plan below that produces certificates the platform itself will reject.

quizzes.question: Why publish to a pilot group before the whole domain?
answers: A small blast radius proves the template before autoenrollment touches fifty machines in course 1.7
Pilots are a licensing requirement
Templates expire if unused
quizzes.explanation: The fleet course will turn autoenrollment loose at scale. Proving the template on a pilot first is the same test-then-widen habit as the Group Policy work.

lessons.title: Validate enrollment, revocation, and recovery
lessons.summary: Finish from a clean domain client the way a relying system sees it: a pilot machine enrolls on its own, validates against the live publication site, and rejects a certificate you revoke — then the change-triggered scans record what this course did.
objectives: Prove pilot autoenrollment through the published template.
Verify chain building and live revocation retrieval from pki.sbd.test, and prove revocation works.
Schedule the renewals that keep the PKI alive, run the delta scans, and file the evidence.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.3 (identity, DNS and time, and the hardened baseline); verify domain health and internal name resolution.

Prepare separate Windows Server hosts: SBD-ROOTCA01 in a disconnected workgroup, SBD-SUBCA01 joined to sbd.test, and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as a hardened member server at 10.0.30.30 in the Servers OU (course 1.5 moves it, with the issuing CA, to a Tier 0 Servers OU).

Approve the CA names, cryptography, validity periods, publication URLs, administration, backups, and removable-media procedure before installation; confirm the network's service-path register permits HTTP to pki.sbd.test.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the whole PKI: a standalone offline Root CA, an enterprise subordinate/issuing CA, the pki.sbd.test publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01, and template administration on its own seat. The root stays disconnected; approved removable media carries requests and public artifacts. Publication stays plain HTTP by design — clients must be able to fetch revocation data before they can validate any certificate.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Enable the autoenrollment policy for the pilot computer group, refresh policy on a pilot machine, and confirm it receives an SBD Computer Authentication certificate without a human touching the request.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: On that machine, export the public certificate and run the full verification: the chain must reach the approved root and every AIA and CDP URL must answer from pki.sbd.test with current CRL dates — cached success is not evidence of publication.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Enroll a disposable test certificate, revoke only that one, publish an updated issuing CRL, and verify that a fresh client evaluation detects the revocation. Diagnose retrieval or stale-publication problems rather than turning off revocation checks.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Record owners and reminders for root and issuing CRL publication, certificate renewal, backup, and an isolated recovery rehearsal. Schedule offline root ceremonies early enough to transfer and publish replacement CRLs before expiry.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Rescan SBD-SUBCA01 and take SBD-PKI-MGMT01's first baseline with the same benchmark and tool versions as always; the publication site and template changes are the expected deltas.

sections.heading: Step 6
sections.body: File the course evidence: enrollment output, urlfetch and revocation results, template records, renewal owners, and the scan set — the PKI chapter is finished.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\pilot.cer
# After revoking the disposable test certificate and publishing the new CRL:
certutil -urlfetch -verify test.cer

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The pilot enrolls hands-free and verifies with live retrieval from pki.sbd.test; after revocation and publication the test certificate is rejected for the expected reason; both VLAN 30 hosts have current, attributed scan results.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Finish the PKI checklist with the pilot's certificate details, urlfetch and revocation results, renewal dates and recovery owners, and the delta-scan comparison for SUBCA01 plus the PKI-MGMT01 baseline.
