quizzes.question: What does a hands-free pilot enrollment prove?
answers: Template permissions, autoenrollment policy, the CA, DNS, and the network path all agree — the whole chain works
Only that Group Policy refreshed
That the root CA is online
quizzes.explanation: Autoenrollment succeeds only when every layer this path has built cooperates — which is exactly why it is the closing test.

quizzes.question: A valid certificate fails because its CRL cannot be retrieved. What is the next step?
answers: Fix and retest the publication or reachability problem
Disable revocation checking for all clients
Copy the root private key to the client
quizzes.explanation: Reliable revocation publication is part of the service. Bypassing the check conceals the failed dependency.

quizzes.question: Why schedule offline root ceremonies ahead of CRL expiry?
answers: A replacement CRL must be transferred and published before the old one expires
The root certificate expires monthly
Clients delete their trust store on expiry
quizzes.explanation: If the root CRL lapses, revocation checking fails across the hierarchy. Manual transfer takes lead time, so it is scheduled early.

quizzes.question: Which hosts get scanned at the end of this course?
answers: Only the pilot workstation
SBD-SUBCA01 (rescan) and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (first baseline)
The offline root over the network
quizzes.explanation: The cadence is change-triggered: the CA changed and a new host joined, so one rescan and one baseline.

recap: Pilot autoenrollment works end to end, with live revocation retrieval from pki.sbd.test.
A revoked test certificate is rejected for the expected reason.

lessons.title: Design the tiers and the address plan
lessons.summary: Tiering is one sentence with teeth: credentials that control a tier never touch a less-trusted one. Write that policy against the OU structure, then plan the DHCP scope the fleet will live in — both before any host is built.
objectives: Define the tiers and map each to systems, OUs, and admin accounts.
Write the credential rule each tier enforces.
Plan the VLAN 80 DHCP scope, options, and relay.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.4: the finished two-tier PKI with its publication site and templates, plus course 1.3's OU structure with the Admin OU in place. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation, with its access control list (ACL) register, are already in place.

Provision Windows Server hosts for SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10) and the three administration systems in VLAN 60: AdminJumpBox01 (.10), SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (.20), SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (.30).

Decide the privileged accounts: separate admin identities per tier, never daily-driver accounts with admin rights.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the control plane before the fleet exists: DHCP for the workstation VLAN, and a tiered administration model where privileged sessions only ever start from dedicated hosts. The model's rule is strict — the jump systems administer; they browse nothing, read no mail, and accept no inbound sessions from user space.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Define three tiers against what exists, using Microsoft's rule: anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Tier 0 is the identity and trust fabric (DCs, both CAs, PKI-MGMT01) plus what controls it — the hypervisor hosts and their console, the core router's management, and the DC-facing parts of the tools that patch, protect, scan, monitor, and back up the DCs. Tier 1 is the member servers; Tier 2 the user endpoints. Map each tier to its OUs: Tier 0 to the Domain Controllers OU plus a new Tier 0 Servers OU for SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (lesson 4 moves them out of the Servers OU), Tier 1 to the Servers OU, and Tier 2 to the Workstations OU.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Write the credential rule per tier: a Tier 0 account signs in only on Tier 0 systems and AdminJumpBox01; Tier 1 admins work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; Tier 2 from SBD-ADMIN-PC01. The audit custodian uses separate accounts and sessions on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 that ordinary server operators cannot use. Each administrator gets separate per-tier accounts — the daily account holds no admin rights anywhere.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Plan the DHCP design: scope 10.0.80.100–199 for the workstation VLAN — 100 addresses, room for the 50 PCs, the test clients, and replacement machines whose old leases have not yet expired — with options for router 10.0.80.1, the two DCs as DNS, and the sbd.test domain; the core router relays VLAN 80 broadcasts to SBD-DHCP01; everything else stays static.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Add the register rows this course needs: VLAN 60 to each tier's management ports (rules A01–A04 in Inside the Network), DHCP relay from the core to SBD-DHCP01 (F04), and explicit denies from VLAN 80 into VLAN 60 — user space never initiates toward the admin plane.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Capture the design inputs: OU targets and current account separation.
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins' | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The tier map names systems, OUs, admin hosts, and accounts for every tier; the DHCP plan is written; and the register has the new permit and deny rows with owners.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the tier access matrix, the per-administrator account plan, the DHCP scope design, and the updated register rows.

quizzes.question: What is the one-sentence tiering rule?
answers: Admins should use strong passwords
Credentials that control a tier never sign in to a less-trusted tier
Every admin needs Domain Admin rights
quizzes.explanation: Everything else in the model — hosts, OUs, logon policies — exists to enforce that single sentence.

quizzes.question: Why does each administrator get separate per-tier accounts?
answers: So a credential captured on a lower tier cannot open a higher one
Licensing counts accounts per tier
Password policies require it
quizzes.explanation: Credential theft travels with sign-ins. Separate accounts bound what any one capture is worth.

quizzes.question: Which direction does the register explicitly deny?
answers: Admin VLAN to the tiers it manages
DCs to anything
User VLAN 80 initiating into the admin VLAN 60
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane reaches down to manage; user space never reaches up. The deny row makes that a logged fact, not an intention.

quizzes.question: SBD-WSUS01 approves the updates the domain controllers install. Which tier administers the domain controllers' update ring?
answers: Tier 1, because WSUS is a member server
Tier 0, because anything that can push code to a DC can control it
Tier 2, because updates start on workstations
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's tier model treats systems that patch, scan, monitor, protect, back up, or host Tier 0 as Tier 0. The DC-facing scope of a tool belongs to Tier 0 even when the server itself sits in a member-server VLAN.

recap: Three tiers, each with its systems, OU, admin host, and accounts.
The credential rule is written before any host enforces it.
DHCP scope, options, relay, and register rows are planned.

lessons.title: Build SBD-DHCP01 and the relay
lessons.summary: Addressing is the first service fifty machines will ask for. Build the DHCP server, authorize it in the directory so rogue servers stand out, and relay VLAN 80's broadcasts through the core.
objectives: Install and authorize the DHCP role on SBD-DHCP01.
Create the VLAN 80 scope with the planned options.
Configure the core relay and prove a lease end to end.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.4: the finished two-tier PKI with its publication site and templates, plus course 1.3's OU structure with the Admin OU in place. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation, with its access control list (ACL) register, are already in place.

Provision Windows Server hosts for SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10) and the three administration systems in VLAN 60: AdminJumpBox01 (.10), SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (.20), SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (.30).

Decide the privileged accounts: separate admin identities per tier, never daily-driver accounts with admin rights.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the control plane before the fleet exists: DHCP for the workstation VLAN, and a tiered administration model where privileged sessions only ever start from dedicated hosts. The model's rule is strict — the jump systems administer; they browse nothing, read no mail, and accept no inbound sessions from user space.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Install the DHCP role on SBD-DHCP01 in the Servers OU and complete directory authorization — an unauthorized Windows DHCP server refuses to serve domain networks, the directory's built-in check against rogue DHCP servers.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create the IPv4 scope 10.0.80.100–199 with the planned options: router 10.0.80.1, DNS 10.0.10.10 and 10.0.10.11, domain sbd.test. Leave every other VLAN static as designed.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Configure dynamic DNS updates using a dedicated low-privilege credential so client records register securely in the sbd.test zone from course 1.2.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Enable the DHCP relay on the core router's VLAN 80 interface toward 10.0.20.10, confirm the register row (F04) permits it, then pull a lease with a temporary test VM in VLAN 80 and watch its A record appear.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-DhcpServerInDC
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope | Select-Object ScopeId, StartRange, EndRange, State
Get-DhcpServerv4OptionValue -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object OptionId, Value
Resolve-DnsName sbd-test80.sbd.test

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The server shows as authorized, the scope serves the planned range and options through the relay, and the test client's secure dynamic DNS record exists on both DCs.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the authorization output, scope and option configuration, the relay setting on the core, and the test lease with its DNS registration.

quizzes.question: What does directory authorization of a DHCP server give you?
answers: Faster leases
A built-in check that makes unauthorized Windows DHCP servers refuse to serve the domain
Larger scopes
quizzes.explanation: Authorization is the directory's rogue-DHCP control — a one-click setting with a real security story behind it.

quizzes.question: Why does the relay exist at all?
answers: DHCP broadcasts do not cross the router, so the core forwards VLAN 80's requests to the server in VLAN 20
It encrypts DHCP traffic
Relays make addresses permanent
quizzes.explanation: Broadcasts stop at the VLAN boundary. The relay is the deliberate, registered exception that carries them to SBD-DHCP01.

quizzes.question: Why use a dedicated credential for dynamic DNS updates?
answers: The server cannot update DNS otherwise
It speeds up record creation
Record ownership and updates trace to one low-privilege identity instead of a powerful computer account
quizzes.explanation: Secure updates from course 1.2 are only as accountable as the identity writing them — a scoped credential keeps that clean.

recap: SBD-DHCP01 is authorized, scoped, and serving through the relay.
Options hand out the gateway, both DCs, and the domain.
A test lease proved addressing and secure DNS registration together.

lessons.title: Build the administration systems
lessons.summary: Privileged work gets dedicated, hardened seats: one jump host for Tier 0, one workstation for server administration, one for endpoint administration — each in the Admin OU, each doing nothing else.
objectives: Link the hardening policies to the Admin OU's computer sub-OUs, then build the three VLAN 60 systems into them.
Keep them single-purpose: hardened, minimal, no user-space services.
Register and restrict their management paths.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.4: the finished two-tier PKI with its publication site and templates, plus course 1.3's OU structure with the Admin OU in place. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation, with its access control list (ACL) register, are already in place.

Provision Windows Server hosts for SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10) and the three administration systems in VLAN 60: AdminJumpBox01 (.10), SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (.20), SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (.30).

Decide the privileged accounts: separate admin identities per tier, never daily-driver accounts with admin rights.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the control plane before the fleet exists: DHCP for the workstation VLAN, and a tiered administration model where privileged sessions only ever start from dedicated hosts. The model's rule is strict — the jump systems administer; they browse nothing, read no mail, and accept no inbound sessions from user space.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Create two computer sub-OUs under the Admin OU — Admin Servers for AdminJumpBox01 and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Admin Workstations for SBD-ADMIN-PC01 — and link course 1.3's Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) to them before any seat joins: the member-server policies to Admin Servers and the Windows client policies from the same package to Admin Workstations. Course 1.3 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so without this step the seats would boot unhardened.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Build AdminJumpBox01, SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and SBD-ADMIN-PC01 as clean Windows Server (or Windows client, for the endpoint seat) installs and join each into its sub-OU, so the hardening applies from first boot.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Strip them to purpose: no browsing to anything but internal admin interfaces, no mail, no file shares hosted, and the management tools for exactly their tier — Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) on the server seats, endpoint tooling on the PC seat.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Register the management paths: VLAN 60 to Tier 0 and Tier 1 ports (remote desktop 3389, remote management 5985–5986, AD Web Services 9389 to the domain controllers, SSH 22 for the domain-joined Linux servers) from the specific admin host each tier allows, and the router's management on VLAN 100 from AdminJumpBox01 only. Keep the VLAN 80 → VLAN 60 deny from lesson 1 in force.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Require the admin hosts' own local firewalls to accept management inbound from nowhere — sessions originate here, they never terminate here. On both domain controllers, scope the existing Remote Desktop, Windows Remote Management, and Active Directory Web Services firewall rules to AdminJumpBox01 and VLAN 10: allow rules add up, so a new, narrower rule would not restrict the broad ones already enabled.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Admin Servers,OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Admin Workstations,OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 5985
gpresult /r /scope:computer

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: All three hosts sit in their Admin sub-OUs with the STIG GPOs linked there and applied, management ports answer from the correct admin host per tier, and nothing in user space can open a session toward VLAN 60.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record each host's build sheet, OU placement, the sub-OU GPO links, gpresult output, and the register rows for its permitted management paths.

quizzes.question: Why do the admin hosts run nothing but administration?
answers: Extra software costs licenses
Every extra capability — mail, browsing, documents — is a way to phish or poison the most valuable sessions on the network
Admin tools conflict with browsers
quizzes.explanation: These hosts carry privileged credentials. Minimizing what runs on them minimizes what can steal from them.

quizzes.question: Which way do management sessions flow?
answers: From the admin hosts outward to their tier — never inbound to the admin hosts
In both directions equally
From workstations to the jump box
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane originates; it never serves. Inbound-nothing is what keeps a compromised endpoint from riding into VLAN 60.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG GPOs to the Admin sub-OUs before the seats join?
answers: The seats cannot join the domain otherwise
The OU name requires it
Course 1.3 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so the seats would otherwise boot unhardened
quizzes.explanation: Policy follows links, not names. Linking first means each seat is STIG-configured from its first boot, before it ever does privileged work.

recap: Three single-purpose admin seats, hardened from first boot.
Management flows outward only; VLAN 60 accepts nothing inbound.
Every management path is a register row.

lessons.summary: The tier rule becomes real when the directory refuses the wrong sign-in. Give Tier 0 servers their own OU first, deny privileged logons on lower tiers by policy, protect the highest accounts, and make the refusal something you can show in a log.
objectives: Move the Tier 0 member servers into their own OU before any deny policy lands.
Enforce per-tier sign-in restrictions with Group Policy logon rights, and record the one network-logon exception.
Protect Tier 0 accounts and prove a cross-tier sign-in is denied and logged.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.4: the finished two-tier PKI with its publication site and templates, plus course 1.3's OU structure with the Admin OU in place. The network's routing and default-deny segmentation, with its access control list (ACL) register, are already in place.

Provision Windows Server hosts for SBD-DHCP01 (10.0.20.10) and the three administration systems in VLAN 60: AdminJumpBox01 (.10), SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (.20), SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (.30).

Decide the privileged accounts: separate admin identities per tier, never daily-driver accounts with admin rights.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the control plane before the fleet exists: DHCP for the workstation VLAN, and a tiered administration model where privileged sessions only ever start from dedicated hosts. The model's rule is strict — the jump systems administer; they browse nothing, read no mail, and accept no inbound sessions from user space.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Create the Tier 0 Servers OU (OU=Tier 0 Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test) with deletion protection, link course 1.3's member-server STIG GPOs to it so nothing loses its hardening, and move SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 there. Both are Tier 0, and the Servers OU is about to deny Tier 0 sign-ins — left there, they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Create one tier logon GPO for the Servers OU — now Tier 1 only — and one for the Workstations OU, and never link either to the Domain Controllers or Tier 0 Servers OUs. User rights don't merge across GPOs: for each right, the highest-precedence GPO that sets it wins, so each list repeats the entries course 1.3's STIG GPO sets for that right (such as Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins), and the tier GPO links above the STIG GPO. On the Servers OU, give the Tier 0 admin group (SBD Tier 0 Admins in this sample) Deny log on locally, Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services, Deny log on as a batch job, and Deny log on as a service. On the Workstations OU, give both the Tier 0 and Tier 1 groups those four denies plus Deny access to this computer from the network.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: On the Servers OU, set Deny access to this computer from the network — the Tier 0 group plus the STIG's entries — in a separate GPO that excludes the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group through security filtering (deny Apply group policy). Course 1.8 adds SBD-WSUS01 and SBD-EPO01 to that group, so those two keep only the STIG's own setting. From AdminJumpBox01, Tier 0 manages the domain controllers' WSUS update ring and their agent policy in Trellix ePolicy Orchestrator (ePO) through those two consoles, using Tier 0 task accounts outside Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins (which the STIG denies network logon on member servers); a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server. Record the exception — the two servers, the accounts, the reason, and its owner — in the course 1.3 exception record.

sections.heading: Step 4

quizzes.question: What turns the tier rule from policy into enforcement?
answers: An email to administrators
Deny-logon rights applied by GPO at each lower tier's OU
Renaming the admin accounts
quizzes.explanation: The OU-linked deny rights are the mechanism: the directory itself refuses the out-of-tier sign-in.

quizzes.question: What does Protected Users membership buy a Tier 0 account?
answers: Faster sign-ins
Exemption from password changes
The domain refuses its weaker authentication paths, shrinking what a credential thief can replay
quizzes.explanation: Protected Users trades convenience for resistance — appropriate exactly for the accounts whose theft ends the network.

quizzes.question: Why does a break-glass account exist outside the deny policies?
answers: So a policy mistake cannot lock every administrator out — and its sealed, alarmed use keeps the exception honest
Because every admin wants one
Deny policies cannot apply to more than ten accounts
quizzes.explanation: Strict tiering needs one documented escape hatch. Sealing and alarming it is what keeps the hatch from becoming a habit.

quizzes.question: Why do SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 move out of the Servers OU before the deny policy is linked?
answers: The Servers OU has reached its size limit
They are Tier 0: the Servers OU now denies Tier 0 sign-ins, so they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems
Certificate Services cannot run in an OU with linked policies
quizzes.explanation: Tier follows control, not hostname. Systems that control Tier 0 need an OU where Tier 0 can sign in and the lower-tier denies never apply.

quizzes.question: Why may Tier 0 still use a network logon on SBD-WSUS01 and SBD-EPO01?
answers: Tier 0 manages the DC update ring and DC agent policy there, and a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server
Network logons are never logged
Those two servers are Tier 0 systems
quizzes.explanation: Interactive, Remote Desktop, batch, and service logons leave reusable credentials behind; a Kerberos network logon does not, and Protected Users accounts cannot be delegated. The exception is narrow, named, and recorded.

lessons.summary: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: scheduled archives from the collector, hashed on arrival, readable by few, deletable by process only.
objectives: Archive the collector's logs to the repository on schedule.
Hash and catalog every archive on arrival.
Enforce the read-few, delete-by-process-only access model.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.5: the admin plane exists, and this course's systems are managed only from VLAN 60.

Provision SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) as Windows Server, SBD-SPLUNK01 (10.0.50.10) on Linux joined to the sbd.test domain with its time service (chrony or ntpd) pointed at both domain controllers, and SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40) as Windows Server joined to the domain.

Have the network's service-path register ready for the new rows: event forwarding to the collector, syslog from the core router, and the forwarder path into the analysis system.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the model's collect → protect → analyze chain before the fleet arrives, so every later system is observed from its first boot. Collection is configuration you can show; protection is permissions and retention you can defend; analysis is a search someone actually runs.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Create the archival job: on schedule, the collector exports its Forwarded Events and syslog intake to dated archive files and transfers them to SBD-AUDIT01's repository share — the only inbound write path the repository allows.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: On arrival, hash each archive and append the hash to a catalog kept with the archives; an archive whose hash no longer matches is a finding, not a file.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Set the permissions to match lesson 1's decision: the archival process writes, a named auditors group reads, and no interactive account holds delete rights — retention-driven deletion runs as its own documented, logged process, administered only under the audit custodian's separate accounts.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Fill in the AU table with what now exists: where each stage's data lives, its retention clock, and who can touch it — this table is the kind of artifact course 2.2 shows joining the Body of Evidence for the audit controls.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ChildItem \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime -First 5
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive\*.evtx | Select-Object -First 3
icacls \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Dated archives arrive on schedule with catalog hashes that verify, the permission listing matches the access model exactly, and the AU table reflects reality.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the archival job definition, the hash catalog excerpt, the permissions output, and the completed AU table.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Wecutil (Windows Event Collector)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/wecutil

NIST · SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security controls (AU family)
https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final

quizzes.question: What does the hash catalog actually protect against?
answers: Disk space exhaustion
Silent modification — an archive that no longer matches its recorded hash announces itself as tampered or corrupted
Slow searches
quizzes.explanation: Integrity is only provable if you recorded what intact looked like. The catalog is that record.

quizzes.question: How does anything ever get deleted from the repository?
answers: Any administrator's right-click
The analysis system prunes it
Only the documented, logged retention process
quizzes.explanation: The point of the repository is surviving its administrators. Deletion exists — as a process with a log, never a privilege.

quizzes.question: Where does the AU table go after this course?
answers: Into the Body of Evidence for the audit controls — course 2.2 shows how artifacts like it are organized
Back into course 1.1, retroactively
Nowhere — it is decorative
quizzes.explanation: Where the records live, how long, and who reads them is precisely what the audit control family asks an assessor to verify.

recap: Archives land on schedule and prove their own integrity.
Readers are named; deletion is a process, not a right.
The AU table is written for the authorization path.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 puts a working copy in front of an analyst.

lessons.title: Analyze in SBD-SPLUNK01
lessons.summary: Analysis earns its place with three working searches and one alert: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself.
objectives: Index the collector's streams into the analysis system.
Build the first three searches against real events.
Create one alert with a named responder.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.5: the admin plane exists, and this course's systems are managed only from VLAN 60.

Provision SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) as Windows Server, SBD-SPLUNK01 (10.0.50.10) on Linux joined to the sbd.test domain with its time service (chrony or ntpd) pointed at both domain controllers, and SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40) as Windows Server joined to the domain.

Have the network's service-path register ready for the new rows: event forwarding to the collector, syslog from the core router, and the forwarder path into the analysis system.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the model's collect → protect → analyze chain before the fleet arrives, so every later system is observed from its first boot. Collection is configuration you can show; protection is permissions and retention you can defend; analysis is a search someone actually runs.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Install the analysis platform on SBD-SPLUNK01 and bring in the collector's two streams — the forwarded Windows events and the router syslog — over the registered forwarder path; the repository stays out of this flow by design.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Build search one: failed sign-ins (event 4625) involving the tier admin accounts, grouped by source host — the tiering course's denials now have a dashboard.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Build search two: router denies by source VLAN and destination port — the network boundary, now trending; and search three: time-service events and offsets, so clock drift surfaces before Kerberos complains.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Turn the first search into an alert with a threshold, a named responder from the admin plane, and a written first-response step — an alert nobody owns is a log entry with extra steps. Console access to all of this: VLAN 60 only, per the handoff.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Test-NetConnection SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test -Port 9997
# In the analysis console, confirm the three saved searches return today's events
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625} -MaxEvents 3 | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both streams index with correct timestamps, the three searches return real current events, and the alert fires in a test with its responder and first step documented.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the input configuration, each search with a result sample, and the alert definition with its responder.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
Microsoft · Use Windows Event Forwarding to help with intrusion detection
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/use-windows-event-forwarding-to-assist-in-intrusion-detection

Splunk · product documentation
https://docs.splunk.com/Documentation

quizzes.question: Why does the repository stay out of the analysis flow?
answers: The protected copy's integrity never depends on the search tier — analysis reads the working stream, not the record
Splunk cannot read archives
Repositories are read-only hardware
quizzes.explanation: Lesson 1's separation, now visible in the plumbing: question the working copy freely; the record stays untouched.

quizzes.question: What makes an alert real rather than decorative?
answers: A red icon
A named responder and a written first step
Firing at least hourly
quizzes.explanation: Detection without ownership is noise. The responder and the first step are what turn a search into a control.

quizzes.question: Why is a time-health search in the first three?
answers: Clocks are easy to chart
Dashboards need a third panel
Drift breaks Kerberos quietly — course 1.2 set up the clock, this search watches it
quizzes.explanation: The pipeline watches the dependencies the network actually has. Time is one failure that looks like everything else until you chart it.

recap: Two streams indexed; the protected record untouched.
Three searches answer real questions from day one.
One alert, one responder, one written first step.
lessons.next: The final lesson proves the chain end to end and runs the scans.

lessons.title: Prove the chain and delta scan
lessons.summary: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the repository's next archive, and the analyst's screen — then the cadence scans close the course.
objectives: Trace a test event through all three stages.
Verify the router-deny stream the same way.
Baseline the new hosts and file the course evidence.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete course 1.5: the admin plane exists, and this course's systems are managed only from VLAN 60.

Provision SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) as Windows Server, SBD-SPLUNK01 (10.0.50.10) on Linux joined to the sbd.test domain with its time service (chrony or ntpd) pointed at both domain controllers, and SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40) as Windows Server joined to the domain.

Have the network's service-path register ready for the new rows: event forwarding to the collector, syslog from the core router, and the forwarder path into the analysis system.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course builds the model's collect → protect → analyze chain before the fleet arrives, so every later system is observed from its first boot. Collection is configuration you can show; protection is permissions and retention you can defend; analysis is a search someone actually runs.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Generate the test event: one failed sign-in on a DC with a wrong password for a tier admin account. Find it in the DC's Security log, in Forwarded Events on the collector, flag it for the next archive's verification on the repository, and watch the alert fire in analysis.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Repeat with the boundary: probe one unregistered port, then find that deny in the syslog stream and in search two — the boundary's evidence pair — attempt and deny — now assembles itself.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Run the cadence: first baselines for SBD-SYSLOG01, SBD-AUDIT01, and SBD-SPLUNK01 (Windows hosts with the standard benchmark; SBD-SPLUNK01 runs Linux, so scan it with the DISA STIG benchmark for its distribution), plus a DC rescan for the audit-policy deltas.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: File the end-to-end trace as this course's signature evidence and write the handoff: the fleet course inherits a pipeline that will see its first domain join happen.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\*

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The test event appears at every stage with consistent timestamps, the deny trace matches, the new hosts have baselines, and the DC rescan deltas are attributed to the audit policy.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the four-stage trace of the test event, the deny trace, the scan set, and the handoff note to course 1.7.

NIST · SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security controls (AU family)
https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final

quizzes.question: What does the single traced event prove that stage-by-stage checks don't?
answers: That events have timestamps
That the stages connect — one real event surviving source to analyst is the pipeline working as a system
That 4625 exists
quizzes.explanation: Components can each pass while the chain fails. The traced event is the integration test.

quizzes.question: How is SBD-SPLUNK01, a domain-joined Linux server, scanned in this lab?
answers: It is exempt from evidence
With the Windows Server benchmark anyway
With the DISA STIG benchmark for its Linux distribution, on the same cadence as the Windows servers
quizzes.explanation: Linux distributions have their own DISA STIGs and Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) content. A domain-joined Linux server is held to the same scan cadence as every other server.

quizzes.question: Why insist the pipeline exists before the fleet course?
answers: So fifty domain joins happen in view of the pipeline — observed from the first boot instead of retrofitted later
Fleets cannot join without Splunk
DHCP requires a SIEM
quizzes.explanation: The ordering argument of this whole path: build the watcher, then the watched. Course 1.7 arrives to a network already paying attention.

recap: One event, four stages, consistent timestamps — the chain is real.
Boundary denies assemble their own evidence now.
Baselines, rescans, and the handoff to course 1.7 close the course.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.6. Course 1.7 brings in the fifty-workstation fleet — watched, addressed, and policy-managed from first boot.

lessons.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
lessons.summary: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.
objectives: Finalize the reference image and naming plan for fifty endpoints.
Create a least-privilege join account scoped to the Workstations OU.
Link the Windows client STIG policies and the workstation firewall policy to the Workstations OU before any join.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.6: working PKI services, DHCP with its relay, the tiered admin plane, and the logging pipeline, on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.

Prepare a patched Windows reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU, the container redirects from course 1.3, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, from the course 1.3 package, are ready to link.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Finalize the Windows reference image: current patches via the approved media process, no preinstalled extras, and a generalized state so each clone takes its own identity. Record the image version and hash — it is the fleet's common ancestor and belongs in evidence.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Write the naming and rollout plan: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50, addressed by the course 1.5 DHCP scope, joined in waves (pilot of three, then batches) rather than all fifty at once.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create a dedicated domain-join account delegated only the create-computer-objects right on the Workstations OU — no broader privilege rides along with fifty join operations. The course 1.3 redirect already guarantees machines land in that OU.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Link the DISA Windows client STIG policies from the course 1.3 package to the Workstations OU now, so the very first pilot boots into the hardened state — and note that the Windows client's own secure defaults will already satisfy some checks, just as Windows Server's did.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Create the workstation firewall GPO (SBD Workstation Firewall in this sample) on the Workstations OU: Windows Defender Firewall on for every profile with inbound traffic blocked by default, and inbound rules that allow SMB (TCP 445), Remote Desktop (TCP 3389), and remote management (TCP 5985–5986) only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 at 10.0.60.30 — course 1.8 adds SBD-NESSUS01 for credentialed scans. No rule allows SMB or Remote Desktop between workstations: traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router, so this policy, not the core router's rules, enforces the register's peer denies.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\Win11-Reference.vhdx
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation Firewall' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-firewall.html

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The image is hashed and recorded, the join account holds only the delegated right on the Workstations OU, and the STIG and firewall GPO links show on that OU before any machine exists in it.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the image record with its hash, the naming and wave plan, the delegation report for the join account, the OU's GPO inheritance output, and the firewall GPO report.

sections.heading: Source documentation
sections.body:
DISA · STIG Group Policy Objects package
https://www.cyber.mil/stigs/gpo

Microsoft · Configure Windows Firewall rules with Group Policy
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/network-security/windows-firewall/configure

NIST · SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security controls
https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final

quizzes.question: Why does the join account get only create-computer rights on one OU?
answers: Join operations fail with more rights
Fifty joins should carry the least privilege possible — a stolen join credential then creates computer objects, nothing more
Delegation is faster than Domain Admin
quizzes.explanation: Scale multiplies exposure. Scoping the account bounds what the rollout's most-used credential is worth to an attacker.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG policies before the first machine joins?
answers: So every endpoint's first boot is already the hardened state — no window where an unmanaged machine exists
GPO links expire if unused
The OU cannot be created otherwise
quizzes.explanation: The redirect lands them in the OU, and the pre-linked policy means compliance from minute one — the course 1.3 design, now paying off at scale.

quizzes.question: What makes the reference image part of the evidence?
answers: Images are always evidence
It contains the domain password
Its recorded version and hash are what make fifty 'identical' endpoints a claim you can verify
quizzes.explanation: A configuration record for the fleet starts with the common ancestor. The hash is how an assessor — or future you — confirms descent.

quizzes.question: What stops one workstation from opening SMB or Remote Desktop to another?
answers: The router's access control lists
Each PC's own firewall, set by the workstation firewall GPO — traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router
Nothing until course 1.8
quizzes.explanation: Two PCs in VLAN 80 talk through the access switch, so the router never sees their traffic. Each PC's Windows Defender Firewall enforces the register's peer denies, which Inside the Network shows as rules D01 and D02.

recap: One hashed image, one naming plan, waves instead of a big bang.
The join credential can create computer objects and nothing else.
The Workstations OU is armed with policy before it holds a machine.
Peer SMB and Remote Desktop are blocked by each PC's own firewall, set by policy before the first join.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 joins the pilot and inspects everything a first boot should bring.

lessons.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
lessons.summary: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.
objectives: Join a three-machine pilot with the scoped account.
Verify lease, OU placement, policy, and DNS registration per machine.
Confirm the joins appear in the logging pipeline.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.6: working PKI services, DHCP with its relay, the tiered admin plane, and the logging pipeline, on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.

Prepare a patched Windows reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU, the container redirects from course 1.3, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, from the course 1.3 package, are ready to link.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Deploy SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC03 from the image into VLAN 80, let each take its DHCP lease, and join sbd.test with the delegated account — nothing about the join should require a privileged credential.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Per machine, verify the inheritance chain: the computer object sits in the Workstations OU (the redirect working), gpresult shows the STIG policies applied, and the secure dynamic DNS record exists on both DCs.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Confirm the deny side holds: a pilot machine cannot reach another pilot machine's SMB or RDP — the lesson 1 firewall policy refuses it on the destination PC, because traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router — and cannot open anything toward VLAN 60, which the core router's rules deny at the boundary.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Find the three joins in the logging pipeline: the domain controller events for the computer-account creations should already be on the collector and searchable in analysis — the first machines this network has watched arrive.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration

Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DNSHostName
gpresult /r /scope:computer
Resolve-DnsName SBD-PC01.sbd.test
Test-NetConnection SBD-PC02.sbd.test -Port 445   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: All three pilots sit in the Workstations OU with STIG policy applied and DNS registered, peer SMB/RDP fails as designed, and the join events are visible in analysis.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep each pilot's placement, gpresult, and DNS proof; the peer-deny output; and the analysis search showing the three computer-account creations.

quizzes.question: How does a brand-new machine end up hardened without anyone touching it?
answers: Windows hardens itself completely
Redirect lands it in the Workstations OU, where the pre-linked STIG policies apply at first boot
The DHCP server pushes the STIG
quizzes.explanation: Three courses cooperate in that one moment: the 1.3 redirect, the 1.3 GPO package, and this lesson's pre-linked OU.

quizzes.question: Why test pilot-to-pilot SMB and expect failure?
answers: SMB is removed from Windows
The pilots are in different domains
Each PC's firewall policy denies peer SMB and Remote Desktop — lateral movement inside VLAN 80 is cut at the destination host
quizzes.explanation: Peer traffic is switched inside VLAN 80 and never reaches the router, so the register's peer denies (D01 and D02) are enforced by each PC's own firewall — the policy lesson 1 linked before any join.

quizzes.question: What does seeing the joins in analysis demonstrate?
answers: The ordering worked — the pipeline built in 1.6 observed the fleet's very first machines arriving
That Splunk licenses cover 50 hosts
Nothing; joins are not logged
quizzes.explanation: Build the watcher, then the watched. The pilot's appearance on the analyst's screen is the sequencing argument made visible.

recap: Three pilots: leased, landed, hardened, registered — untouched by hand.
Peer traffic fails by design; the denies are the fleet's first evidence.
The pipeline watched the fleet being born.

lessons.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
lessons.summary: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.
objectives: Prepare the directory schema and permissions for Windows LAPS.
Apply the LAPS policy to the Workstations OU.
Retrieve and rotate a managed password under the tier rules.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.6: working PKI services, DHCP with its relay, the tiered admin plane, and the logging pipeline, on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.

Prepare a patched Windows reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU, the container redirects from course 1.3, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, from the course 1.3 package, are ready to link.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Extend the directory schema for Windows LAPS (Update-LapsADSchema) and grant the Workstations OU's computers the right to update their own password attributes — a one-time Tier 0 action, performed from the jump host and recorded like any schema change.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Grant read access on the managed passwords to the Tier 2 admin group only — exactly the people SBD-ADMIN-PC01 exists for — and nobody else; the tier model decides who may know an endpoint's local secret.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create the LAPS GPO on the Workstations OU: managed built-in administrator, the password complexity and age the plan sets, and post-authentication reset so a used password does not live on.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: On a pilot, confirm the policy applied, retrieve the password from the admin seat, use it once, and watch rotation — one cycle, fully observed, is the proof the other forty-nine inherit.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SBD-PC01 -AsPlainText   # from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, Tier 2 admin
Get-ADComputer SBD-PC01 -Properties msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime | Select-Object Name, msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime
gpresult /r /scope:computer

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The schema holds the LAPS attributes, only the Tier 2 group can read passwords, the policy shows on the pilots, and one retrieve-use-rotate cycle is recorded.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the schema-change record, the permission delegation, the LAPS policy report, and the observed rotation cycle.

quizzes.question: What problem does LAPS remove from a fifty-machine fleet?
answers: Slow sign-ins
One shared local administrator password — where a single capture would open every endpoint
Password complexity rules
quizzes.explanation: Identical images tempt identical secrets. Per-machine rotating passwords make one compromised endpoint worth exactly one endpoint.

quizzes.question: Who may read a managed endpoint password?
answers: Any authenticated user
The machine's primary user

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Add the Network Policy Server role to SBD-DHCP01 and register it in Active Directory. Give it a server certificate with the Server Authentication purpose from the issuing CA. sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Add the VLAN 80 access switch as a RADIUS client with a long, unique shared secret, then create the network policy: wired 802.1X, EAP-TLS only, machine certificates that chain to the approved root and carry the Client Authentication purpose, from the Domain Computers group.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create quarantine VLAN 90 with no gateway and no routes and set it as the ports' failure and guest VLAN, but enable 802.1X on the VLAN 80 access ports in monitor (audit) mode: the switch runs every authentication and reports the result, yet keeps forwarding on VLAN 80 whatever the outcome (vendors name this mode differently). The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain in lesson 6, so enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, with no route to a domain controller. Push the wired 802.1X client settings to the Workstations OU by Group Policy (Wired AutoConfig, EAP-TLS, the approved root as the trusted CA).

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Prove monitor mode with the pilots: each authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs a grant (event 6272), while a failed attempt is logged — as event 6273 when the request reaches NPS — but still forwards on VLAN 80. Add register row F20 with its owner, and confirm the NPS events reach the course 1.6 collector through the existing event forwarding subscription.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: This course keeps the proven state from drifting: updates and software arrive only through controlled channels, every endpoint runs managed protection, and a credentialed scanner turns the course 1.3 cadence into routine. sections.heading: Step 1

sections.heading: Step 2

sections.heading: Step 3

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Install the WSUS role on SBD-WSUS01, scope its products and classifications to what the network actually runs — the Windows Server and Windows client releases in use, and Defender definitions — and nothing speculative. Microsoft announced in September 2024 that WSUS is deprecated and no longer actively developed, but it is still included in Windows Server and supported for production deployments, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Feed it offline: export the needed content on the connected side, hash it, carry it across, and import — the WSUS offline servicing path is the course 1.3 media procedure wearing an update hat.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create WSUS computer groups matching the rings, and link ring GPOs at the OUs: update source SBD-WSUS01, the ring's group assignment, and install/restart windows that respect what each ring does for a living. The critical ring's GPO links to the Domain Controllers and Tier 0 Servers OUs.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Approve one update cycle for the pilot ring only, watch it install and report, then promote the approval ring by ring — the critical ring installs only what two rings already survived. Pilot and broad-ring approvals are Tier 1 work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; critical-ring approvals for the domain controllers and the two Tier 0 servers are Tier 0 work from AdminJumpBox01. Add SBD-WSUS01 to the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group and restart it so the new membership applies: the console reaches the server as a Kerberos network logon, the one Tier 0 logon type course 1.5's deny policy leaves open there, as its exception record states.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-WsusServer | Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' | Select-Object FullDomainName, LastReportedStatusTime
gpresult /r /scope:computer
Get-WindowsUpdateLog -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Every system reports to its ring's group, the pilot ring installed and reported the first approved cycle, and the promotion to later rings followed the written order.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Record the product scope, the offline import with hashes, the ring GPO reports, and the first cycle's per-ring approval and install timeline.

answers: Pretty formatting
Update-on-change plus a scheduled reconciliation against sources that cannot lie — the directory and the leases
Monthly printing

A reason to restart DHCP

quizzes.question: Why credentialed scans rather than unauthenticated ones?
answers: They run quieter on the network
Logged-in checks see the real configuration state — patch levels and settings — instead of guessing from the outside
Credentials are required by law
quizzes.explanation: The cadence wants configuration truth, which only an authenticated look provides; the scan account's scoping and logging keep that power honest.

quizzes.question: Where does a scanner finding end up?

In the scanner only

courses.subtitle: Files, database, licensing & web — by documented paths
courses.description: Give the users what the network exists for: SBD-FS01's role-based shares over verified SMB security, SBD-WEB01 serving internal HTTPS from a hardened, domain-joined Linux Apache, SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API, and SBD-SQL01 running as a managed identity behind exactly one caller — every hop a documented, proven register row.

lessons.title: Design the service paths and identities
lessons.summary: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.
objectives: Write the register rows for every business service path.
Choose managed service identities instead of password accounts.
Define the access groups that will own each service's data.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.8: working PKI services and the watched, managed network with the ring/source rules in force, on the routed, segmented VLANs.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20), SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40, Linux with Apache, joined to the sbd.test domain with SSSD like SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01).

Have the network's service-path register and the course 1.4 SBD Server Authentication template ready — every service here gets a documented path and a real certificate.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the service-path rows: fleet to FS01 (SMB 445); fleet to APPS01 on its licensing port, recorded per application; fleet to WEB01 (HTTPS 443); WEB01 to APPS01 for the application API (HTTPS 443); and APPS01 — and only APPS01 — to SQL01 (TCP 1433 with TLS). Add an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01: the web tier has no database dependency. All four servers share VLAN 40, so the router never sees their traffic to each other — each server's host firewall enforces those rows. Everything else toward VLAN 40 stays denied, including endpoint-to-SQL directly.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Register WEB01's Linux maintenance rows as well: packages from SBD-REPO01 only (HTTP with GPG-signed packages) and syslog over TLS to the collector, SBD-SYSLOG01 (TCP 6514) — the same paths the other domain-joined Linux servers, SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01, use. Course 1.8's repository row named only those two because WEB01 did not exist yet.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Choose the service identities: group managed service accounts (gMSAs) for the SQL and application services, so passwords rotate themselves — and note delegated managed service accounts, introduced in the newest Windows Server release, as the migration path for any legacy service account this lab later inherits.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Create the access groups under the course 1.3 Groups OU — per-share and per-application role groups — because permissions will be granted to roles, never to named humans.

sections.heading: Step 5
sections.body: Request the server certificates through the course 1.4 process: one SBD Server Authentication certificate each for SQL01, APPS01 (for its application API), and WEB01, enrolled from the template, with the publication site serving their revocation story.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Enabled
Get-ADGroup -SearchBase 'OU=Groups,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name
Test-NetConnection 10.0.40.20 -Port 1433   # expected before build: TcpTestSucceeded False

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The register carries every service row — the SQL path restricted to APPS01 alone, the WEB01-to-SQL01 deny, and WEB01's repository and syslog rows — the gMSAs and role groups exist, and the three server certificates are issued and recorded.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the service-path rows, the identity and group design, and the certificate enrollment records.

quizzes.question: Who may reach SQL01 on 1433?
answers: Any domain member
WEB01 and APPS01
Only APPS01 — the application tier is the database's whole audience
quizzes.explanation: Browsers talk to the web tier, the web tier calls the application API, and only the application tier queries the database. The register encodes that chain — including an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01 — and denies shortcuts around it.

quizzes.question: Why gMSAs instead of a user account named svc-sql?
answers: The directory manages and rotates the password itself — no human knows it, nothing expires unnoticed
gMSAs run queries faster
Password accounts cannot start services
quizzes.explanation: Service account passwords are a classic standing weakness. Managed accounts remove the password from human hands entirely.

quizzes.question: Why grant access to role groups rather than people?
answers: Groups are alphabetical
Access follows the job: membership changes are one record, and permissions never accumulate on individuals
Permissions cannot hold user names
quizzes.explanation: Role-based access is what makes 'who can touch this data' answerable from group membership instead of archaeology.

recap: Every path is a row; the database hears only SBD-APPS01.
Service identities are managed accounts, not passwords.
Access belongs to roles; certificates are already in hand.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20), SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40, Linux with Apache, joined to the sbd.test domain with SSSD like SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01).

Have the network's service-path register and the course 1.4 SBD Server Authentication template ready — every service here gets a documented path and a real certificate.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-FS01 in the Servers OU and create the planned shares, granting NTFS permissions to the lesson-1 role groups only — share permissions stay simple, the filesystem carries the detail, and no named human appears in an access control list (ACL).

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Enable access-based enumeration so users see only what their roles permit — the quiet UX of least privilege.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Confirm the SMB posture. The newest Windows client release (Pro, Enterprise, and Education) requires SMB signing for both inbound and outbound connections, but the newest Windows Server release requires it only for its own outbound connections — so require signing on SBD-FS01 as well (RequireSecuritySignature in its SMB server configuration), and opt the sensitive share into SMB encryption. Verify both on a live connection from a fleet machine rather than assuming the defaults.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Test as members of two different roles from fleet machines: each sees and opens exactly its shares, the other's are invisible and denied, and the denial lands in the pipeline like every other refusal on this network.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, FolderEnumerationMode, EncryptData   # on FS01
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature   # on FS01: expected True
Get-SmbConnection -ServerName SBD-FS01 | Select-Object ShareName, Dialect, Signed, Encrypted   # on the fleet machine, during the test session
icacls D:\Shares\Projects | Select-String 'SBD'

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Shares grant to role groups only, FS01 requires signing, a live connection from the fleet shows Signed True — or, on the encrypted share, Encrypted True, where Signed reads False even though an encrypted connection is also signed — and the two-role test proves both the access and the invisible-denied behavior.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the share and NTFS permission reports, FS01's signing setting and the live connection's signing/encryption output, and the two-role test record with its pipeline entry.

lessons.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
lessons.summary: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.
objectives: Install the database service under its gMSA.
Bind the SBD Server Authentication certificate for encrypted connections.
Prove the one-caller rule: SBD-APPS01 connects; SBD-WEB01 and the fleet are refused.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.8: working PKI services and the watched, managed network with the ring/source rules in force, on the routed, segmented VLANs.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20), SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40, Linux with Apache, joined to the sbd.test domain with SSSD like SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01).

Have the network's service-path register and the course 1.4 SBD Server Authentication template ready — every service here gets a documented path and a real certificate.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Install the database engine on SBD-SQL01 with the lesson-1 gMSA as its service identity — the install itself demonstrates the managed account working where a password account used to live.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Bind the issued certificate to the instance and require encrypted connections; the chain validates against pki.sbd.test like every other certificate on this network.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Create the application databases with role-based database access for the APPS01 application identity only — least privilege continues inside the engine, not just at its port.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Prove the audience: a connection from APPS01 succeeds encrypted. The same attempt from SBD-WEB01 is refused by SBD-SQL01's host firewall — the two share VLAN 40, so the router never sees it — and one from a fleet machine dies at the router with a deny-log entry. Turn on the host firewall's dropped-packet logging if it is off, so both refusals leave a record.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Get-Service MSSQLSERVER -ComputerName SBD-SQL01 | Select-Object Status
# From SBD-APPS01, the registered caller: expected TcpTestSucceeded True.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433
# From a fleet machine: expected TcpTestSucceeded False.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433
# From SBD-WEB01 (Linux): expected to be refused or time out.
nc -zv SBD-SQL01.sbd.test 1433
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\services\sql01.cer

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The service runs as the gMSA, connections are certificate-encrypted with a validating chain, APPS01's access works by database role, and both direct attempts fail with a record: SBD-WEB01's at SQL01's host firewall, the fleet's at the router.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the service identity proof, the certificate binding and urlfetch output, the database role grants, and APPS01's successful connection paired with both refusals and their log entries.

A diagram of VLAN 40

quizzes.explanation: Same standard as every boundary check: the permit shown working and the deny shown refusing, each with its record.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-WEB01's attempt on SQL01 never reach the router?
answers: The router is offline during the test

Connections encrypt under the lab's own validated chain.
One caller in: SBD-APPS01. SBD-WEB01 is refused at SQL01's host firewall and the fleet at the router.

lessons.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
lessons.summary: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.
objectives: Stand up SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API on their registered paths.
Build the domain-joined Linux Apache server hardened per its DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG), serving HTTPS with the internal certificate.
Prove the full chain: fleet → web → application → database, with the web-to-database shortcut refused.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.4–1.8: working PKI services and the watched, managed network with the ring/source rules in force, on the routed, segmented VLANs.

Provision the VLAN 40 hosts: SBD-FS01 (10.0.40.10), SBD-SQL01 (10.0.40.20), SBD-APPS01 (10.0.40.30), and SBD-WEB01 (10.0.40.40, Linux with Apache, joined to the sbd.test domain with SSSD like SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01).

Have the network's service-path register and the course 1.4 SBD Server Authentication template ready — every service here gets a documented path and a real certificate.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The users finally get what the network exists for: files, licensing, and an internal web application with its application tier and database. The model's rule governs the whole course — permit only documented business service paths — so every service arrives with its register rows, its service identity, and its certificate, and nothing reaches it any other way.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Build SBD-APPS01 in the Servers OU and run both of its services under managed identities: the licensing service, verified from the fleet on its registered vendor port, and the application API on HTTPS 443 with its SBD Server Authentication certificate, answering SBD-WEB01 only. APPS01 is the network's one SQL consumer — and the template for any future service: identity, row, evidence.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Build SBD-WEB01 on Linux and join it to the sbd.test domain with SSSD, as SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01 are joined. Point its packages at SBD-REPO01 only, its syslog over TLS at the collector, and its time service at both domain controllers, and harden the web tier against DISA's Apache guidance — the server's assessable record follows the Linux pattern: hardened configuration exported and hashed, checklist items answered in STIG Viewer.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Install the SBD Server Authentication certificate with its chain and serve the internal application over HTTPS — the 2,048-bit key floor from course 1.4's templates applies here as everywhere.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Prove the chain from a fleet machine: the HTTPS page loads with a validating certificate, and its data travels fleet → WEB01 → APPS01 → SQL01, every hop a register row. Then prove the shortcuts stay shut: a direct attempt from SBD-WEB01 to SQL01 on 1433 is refused by SQL01's host firewall, and the fleet still cannot touch 1433 at all — three courses of design visible in one browser request.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
Test-NetConnection SBD-WEB01.sbd.test -Port 443   # from a fleet machine
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\services\web01.cer
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433   # from the fleet: expected False
# On SBD-WEB01 (Linux): domain membership, the API answers, the database does not.
realm list
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://SBD-APPS01.sbd.test/   # use your application's health path
nc -zv SBD-SQL01.sbd.test 1433   # expected: refused or timed out

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The licensing path works as registered, SBD-WEB01 is domain-joined with SSSD and patches only from SBD-REPO01, the Apache host serves HTTPS with a validating internal chain from a hardened, hashed configuration, and the end-to-end request proves fleet → web → application → database with both shortcuts denied.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep APPS01's identity and path proof, WEB01's domain-join and repository settings, its hardened config export with hashes and checklist, the certificate validation output, the end-to-end chain test, and the refused WEB01-to-SQL01 attempt.

answers: Any public mirror that responds
A USB stick from home
SBD-REPO01 — the one approved source the 1.8 rule named for Linux software
quizzes.explanation: The one-source rule follows software wherever it runs; the web tier installs only what crossed the boundary through the repository, on the row lesson 1 registered for it.

quizzes.question: What is the Apache host's assessable record?
answers: A screenshot of the home page
Its hardened configuration export with hashes plus the answered STIG checklist — the established Linux pattern
Its uptime counter
quizzes.explanation: The router, the repository, and now the web tier: no Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) automation does not mean no evidence standard.

quizzes.question: What does one successful page load from the fleet actually demonstrate?
answers: The whole designed chain — the registered fleet-to-web path, validating internal HTTPS, the web tier's call to the application API, and the application tier's registered path into the database
Only that Apache started
That the fleet can reach the database directly
quizzes.explanation: The request traverses three register rows (fleet to WEB01, WEB01 to APPS01, APPS01 to SQL01) and the PKI in one go — which is why it is the lesson's closing test.

quizzes.question: SBD-WEB01 tries SQL01 directly on 1433. What happens, and why?
answers: It connects, because both servers sit in VLAN 40
SQL01's host firewall refuses it: WEB01 has no database dependency, and APPS01 is the only registered SQL consumer
The router drops it at the core
quizzes.explanation: The web tier reaches data only through the application API. The explicit WEB01-to-SQL01 deny, enforced on SQL01 because both servers share a VLAN, is what keeps a compromised web server from going straight for the database.

recap: APPS01 serves licensing and the application API; WEB01 joins the domain like the other Linux servers.
The web tier is hardened to its guidance and serves the lab's own trust.
One page load proves fleet → web → application → database; the shortcuts stay shut.

courses.subtitle: Backups with custody, one rehearsed restore & the closing record
courses.description: Close the Build path by proving the network can come back: scheduled directory and CA backups under ceremony-grade custody, policy, boundary, logs, and the living records in one hashed catalog, a timed restore rehearsal in isolation, and the recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence.
