lessons.title: Decide what recovery must prove
lessons.summary: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.
objectives: Name the recovery set: what must come back, in what order.
Set the recovery point and time objectives per item.
Decide where backups live and who can touch them.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.9: the full network, its records, and the protected log archive all exist.

Provision a protected backup volume on each server, written only by its backup job, an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords from course 1.1 and the CA key protection decisions from course 1.4 — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course backs up what matters — directory, certificate authority, policy, boundary, and the log record — proves one real restore in isolation, and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Write the recovery set in dependency order — the same order the path built it: the directory first (everything trusts it), then the CA's database and keys, Group Policy, the router configuration, the log archive, and the living records themselves (register, inventory, exception record).

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Set the two numbers per item: how much history may be lost (recovery point) and how long restoration may take (recovery time) — lab-honest values you will actually measure against in lesson 5, not aspirations.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Decide backup placement: each server's protected backup volume is written only by the backup process and readable by the recovery role, and a custodian carries copies to the offline backup cabinet on media — the air-gapped network's version of an off-site copy. There is no network path to the cabinet.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Confirm the standing custody items: the DSRM passwords are sealed and findable, and the root CA's protected backup from the course 1.4 ceremony is accounted for — recovery depends on secrets that must exist before the bad day.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Capture the current protection state before this course changes it.
wbadmin get versions
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object   # this server's protected backup volume

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The recovery set is ordered by dependency with point and time objectives per item, the backup placement and access rules are written, and the DSRM and root-key custody records check out.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the recovery requirements sheet, the objectives table, the placement and access decisions, and the custody verification notes.

https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final

quizzes.question: Why does the directory lead the recovery order?
answers: It has the most data
Everything else authenticates against it — services restored before identity have nothing to trust
Alphabetical order
quizzes.explanation: Recovery order mirrors build order for the same reason: the dependency chain starts at identity.

quizzes.question: What makes a recovery time objective honest?
answers: Making it very small
Leaving it unstated
Setting a value you will actually measure a rehearsal against
quizzes.explanation: Lesson 5 times a real restore. An objective nobody measures is marketing, not a commitment.

quizzes.question: What is the offline media copy for?
answers: Surviving a failure that takes the online backup with it — the air-gapped answer to off-site
Faster restores
Decoration for the evidence binder
quizzes.explanation: Replication and online backups share failure modes with what they protect. One custody-tracked copy stands apart.

recap: The recovery set is ordered by dependency, directory first.
Point and time objectives exist to be measured, not admired.
Backups get a protected home plus one offline, custody-tracked copy.

lessons.title: Back up the directory, on schedule
lessons.summary: System state from both controllers, on a schedule, to the protected target — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.
objectives: Schedule system state backups on both domain controllers.
Verify and catalog each backup with hashes.
Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin for object-level recovery.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.9: the full network, its records, and the protected log archive all exist.

Provision a protected backup volume on each server, written only by its backup job, an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords from course 1.1 and the CA key protection decisions from course 1.4 — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course backs up what matters — directory, certificate authority, policy, boundary, and the log record — proves one real restore in isolation, and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Schedule Windows Server Backup jobs on SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 to each server's protected backup volume, including the system state and all critical volumes (wbadmin's -allCritical) so the same backup also supports a full server (bare-metal) recovery to different hardware — two controllers, two independent backups, because replication is availability and was never recovery (course 1.1's point, now kept).

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: After the first run, verify each backup's completion, record its version identifier, and hash the catalog entry into the evidence set — an unverified backup is a hope with a timestamp.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin (a one-way, forest-level action from the Tier 0 seat, recorded as the change it is) so a deleted user or OU comes back intact without touching system state at all.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Write the restore decision tree: deleted object → Recycle Bin; corrupted DC on its own hardware → system state restore in DSRM (lesson 5's rehearsal); DC whose hardware is gone → full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup; whole-forest loss → the Microsoft forest recovery guide, referenced and staged with the evidence rather than improvised on the day.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
wbadmin get versions
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter {Name -like 'Recycle Bin*'} | Select-Object Name, EnabledScopes
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\backup-catalog.txt

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Both DCs show scheduled, completed system state versions on the protected target, the Recycle Bin reports an enabled scope, and the decision tree names the tool for each failure class.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the backup schedules and version listings, the hashed catalog, the Recycle Bin enablement record, and the restore decision tree.

answers: Replication copies mistakes as faithfully as data; independent backups are the history replication doesn't keep
Backups run faster in pairs
Only one actually holds the directory

quizzes.question: An administrator deletes an OU by mistake. First tool?
answers: Rebuild the forest
The Recycle Bin — object-level restore with attributes intact, no system state needed

answers: A long retention setting
Its file size
Verified completion, a recorded version, and a hashed catalog entry — and eventually a rehearsed restore

lessons.title: Back up the CA, policy, boundary, and records
lessons.summary: The directory is not the only thing the network cannot re-derive: the issuing CA's database and key, the Group Policy set, the router's configuration, the log archive, and the living records each get their protected, cataloged copy.
objectives: Back up the issuing CA's database and key to its protected backup volume under ceremony-grade protection.
Refresh the Group Policy object (GPO) and router configuration backups into the protected set.
Fold the log archive and living records into the same catalog.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.9: the full network, its records, and the protected log archive all exist.

Provision a protected backup volume on each server, written only by its backup job, an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords from course 1.1 and the CA key protection decisions from course 1.4 — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course backs up what matters — directory, certificate authority, policy, boundary, and the log record — proves one real restore in isolation, and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Back up the issuing CA — database and private key — with certutil to SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume (E:\Backups in this sample), never to C:\Evidence: the private key is a secret, and secrets never go into evidence. Protect the key material to the same standard as the course 1.4 ceremony artifacts and record custody; only the backup's hashes and the custody record go into the evidence folder. The root's protected backup already exists from that ceremony and is verified, not duplicated, here.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Refresh the Group Policy backup (the course 1.3 Backup-GPO set, now the whole policy estate) and the router configuration export into the protected target, each hashed into the catalog.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Confirm the log archive's protection already satisfies this course — SBD-AUDIT01's hashed archives are themselves the record — and add the archive catalog to the recovery set so the evidence survives the systems it describes.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Export the living records — register, inventory, exception record, and this course's own sheets — into the set: a recovered network without its records would pass no assessment and teach the wrong lesson.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On SBD-SUBCA01: back up to the protected backup volume, never to the evidence folder.
certutil -backup E:\Backups\SBD-SUBCA01\ca-backup   # prompts for the password that protects the exported key
# Only the hashes and the custody record go into evidence.
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups\SBD-SUBCA01\ca-backup -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\recovery\ca-backup-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\gpo-backup\* | Select-Object -First 6

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The CA backup sits on SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume with key custody recorded and only its hashes in evidence, the policy and router exports are current and hashed, and the catalog covers logs and living records alongside the systems.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the CA backup's hash list and custody record (never the backup itself), the refreshed policy and router exports with hashes, and the complete recovery catalog.

quizzes.question: Why does the CA key backup get ceremony-grade handling?
answers: A copied issuing key is the power to mint trusted certificates — the backup is as sensitive as the CA itself
Keys are large files
certutil requires it
quizzes.explanation: Backups inherit the sensitivity of what they contain. The course 1.4 custody discipline applies to every copy of key material, forever.

quizzes.question: Why do the register, inventory, and exception record join the backup set?
answers: They are the largest files
A restored network without its records has lost its assessable story — the evidence must survive what it evidences
Backups require ten items minimum
quizzes.explanation: This path's real product is a defensible record. Recovery that saves the machines and loses the story saves the wrong half.

quizzes.question: What does this lesson do about the offline root's backup?
answers: Copies it onto the network for convenience
Ignores it
Verifies the ceremony-era backup's custody — it already exists, offline, and stays that way
quizzes.explanation: The root's protection is its isolation. This course checks the promise rather than breaking it with a networked copy.

quizzes.question: Where does the issuing CA's backup go?
answers: Into C:\Evidence, so assessors can inspect it
Onto SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume, with only its hashes and the custody record in evidence
Onto pki.sbd.test, beside the CRLs
quizzes.explanation: The backup holds the CA's private key, and secrets never go into evidence — the DNS course's rule. Evidence records that the backup exists and is intact: its hashes and its custody, not its contents.

recap: CA database and key: backed up to the protected volume, custody recorded, only hashes in evidence.
Policy, boundary, logs, and records all live in one hashed catalog.
The evidence now survives the systems it describes.

lessons.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
lessons.summary: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.
objectives: Define which custodian carries which backup, by tier.
Transfer the copies to offline media with hashes and custody records.
Prove a copy can be found, verified, and returned for a restore.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.9: the full network, its records, and the protected log archive all exist.

Provision a protected backup volume on each server, written only by its backup job, an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords from course 1.1 and the CA key protection decisions from course 1.4 — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course backs up what matters — directory, certificate authority, policy, boundary, and the log record — proves one real restore in isolation, and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Assign custodians by tier: a Tier 0 custodian handles DC system state and the issuing CA's database and key backup; the audit custodian handles the log archive from SBD-AUDIT01; a server custodian handles member-server backups. No one carries a tier they do not hold.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: For each copy, write the media ID, hash the backup on its protected volume, copy it to encrypted removable media, and verify the hash on the media before it leaves the room.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Carry the media to the offline backup cabinet and record the handoff in the custody register: who, what, when, the hashes, and the storage slot. This is the course 1.3 media procedure used for backups.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Pull one copy back as a test: find it from the register, verify its hash, and confirm it is readable. Lesson 5's rehearsal restores from a copy that has made this round trip.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# Hash on the protected volume, then on the media.
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 E:\Backups\SBD-DC02\*.vhdx
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 F:\Media-0012\SBD-DC02\*.vhdx

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: Every item in the recovery set has an offline copy with matching hashes on the volume and the media, a custody entry with a named custodian of the right tier, and one copy has been retrieved and verified.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the custodian assignments, the hash pairs, the custody register entries, and the retrieval test record.

quizzes.question: Who carries the domain controllers' system-state backup to the cabinet?
answers: Any server operator who is free
A Tier 0 custodian
The help desk
quizzes.explanation: A DC backup holds the directory's secrets. Whoever can handle it can rebuild or read the domain, so it stays with Tier 0.

quizzes.question: Why is there no network path to the offline backup cabinet?
answers: So ransomware or an intruder on the network cannot reach or encrypt the copies
Because backups are too large to send
Because NIST forbids network backups
quizzes.explanation: An offline copy survives an attack that takes the whole network. The custody record replaces the network path as the proof of what happened.

quizzes.question: The hash on the media does not match the hash on the volume. What do you do?
answers: Store it anyway and note it
Delete the original
Do not store it; recopy and investigate, because the copy is not trustworthy
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the copy is not the backup you verified. Storing it would put an untrusted copy where you will look on the worst day.

recap: Custodians carry only the backups their tier allows.
Every copy has matching hashes and a custody entry.
A copy has been retrieved and verified before anyone needs it.

lessons.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
lessons.summary: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.
objectives: Restore a DC's system state in Directory Services Restore Mode on the isolated recovery segment.
Measure the restore against the time objective and verify directory health.
Perform and record an object-level Recycle Bin restore.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.body:
Complete courses 1.1–1.9: the full network, its records, and the protected log archive all exist.

Provision a protected backup volume on each server, written only by its backup job, an offline backup cabinet with removable media and a custody register, and an isolated recovery network segment (or host) for the restore rehearsal.

Have the custody records handy: the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) passwords from course 1.1 and the CA key protection decisions from course 1.4 — recovery is where those promises come due.

sections.heading: The lab plan
sections.body: The model's final chapter: a network that cannot come back was never really built. This course backs up what matters — directory, certificate authority, policy, boundary, and the log record — proves one real restore in isolation, and files the tested-recovery evidence the authorization path expects.

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.body: Stage the rehearsal: the isolated recovery segment has no path to the production VLANs — a restored controller believing it is authoritative must never meet the live directory; that isolation rule is written before the restore starts.

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.body: Restore SBD-DC02 from the offline copy retrieved in lesson 4, timing the work from decision to directory-services-running against the lesson-1 objective. A system state restore needs the same server instance — use a copy of SBD-DC02's virtual machine attached only to the isolated segment — started in DSRM: bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair, restart, and sign in with the DSRM password. Restoring to different hardware needs a full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup instead.

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.body: Remove the DSRM boot setting (bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot) and restart normally, then verify the restored directory the course 1.1 way — services, shares, a directory query. Record what the rehearsal taught: steps that surprised you, the measured time, and the decision-tree updates; then tear the rehearsal down completely.

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.body: Back in production, run the everyday restore: delete a disposable test object, bring it back from the Recycle Bin with attributes intact, and file both rehearsals — the big one and the small one — as the tested-recovery evidence.

sections.heading: Inspect your configuration
sections.body:
# On the isolated copy of SBD-DC02: start in DSRM, then sign in with the DSRM password.
bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair
shutdown -t 0 -r
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:<media-volume> -machine:SBD-DC02
wbadmin start systemstaterecovery -version:<version-id> -backupTarget:<media-volume> -machine:SBD-DC02
bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot   # then restart normally
Get-Service NTDS,DNS,Netlogon   # after restart, on the restored controller
Restore-ADObject -Identity <deleted-object-guid>   # production Recycle Bin rehearsal

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.body: The isolated restore ran in DSRM and reached a healthy directory within (or honestly against) the time objective, the DSRM boot setting is removed, the teardown is confirmed, and the production object restore returned the test object intact.

sections.heading: Keep your evidence
sections.body: Keep the timed rehearsal log with its verification output, the lessons-learned and decision-tree updates, the teardown confirmation, and the object-restore record.

quizzes.question: Why must the rehearsal segment be isolated from production?
answers: To make the restore faster
A restored controller carries old directory state — meeting the live forest would inject the past into the present
Isolation is optional for labs
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal's first rule protects production from the rehearsal. Old authoritative state on a live network is its own disaster.

quizzes.question: The restore took longer than the objective. What now?
answers: Hide the timing
Declare the objective met anyway
Record the honest number and either fix the process or revise the objective — both are legitimate; silence is not
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal exists to replace belief with measurement. Either outcome — better process or truer objective — improves the real bad day.

quizzes.question: Why rehearse the Recycle Bin restore too?
answers: The most likely recovery event deserves the same tested-and-recorded treatment as the rare one
It is required before system state restores
Deleted objects expire daily
quizzes.explanation: Recovery evidence should match recovery reality: object-level loss is the common case, so its tool gets proven, not presumed.

quizzes.question: Your recovery host is new hardware. Which restore applies?
answers: A system state restore, exactly as on the original server
A full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup — system state restores are for the same server instance
Copying NTDS.dit across by hand
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's forest recovery guidance calls for a full server recovery when you restore to different hardware or a different operating system instance. A system state restore runs on the original instance, in DSRM.

recap: One real restore, isolated, timed, verified, and torn down.
The measured number replaced the hoped-for one.
The everyday restore is proven alongside the dramatic one.

Run the closing scan snapshot across the finished network.
Hand the complete evidence set to the authorization path.

courses.title: Risk Management Framework
courses.subtitle: Scope, categorization, and control selection
courses.description: Apply the Risk Management Framework (RMF) to the system built in Inside the Network. Establish responsibilities and boundaries, justify mission impacts, and select a defensible control set before developing its Body of Evidence.

materials.title: Interactive authorization course
materials.description: Lessons, evidence examples, and the capstone.

materials.title: Full training catalog · Word
materials.description: Edition 1.4 · 12 modules

lessons.title: 01 · RMF and authorization fundamentals
lessons.summary: Explain the relationship between the RMF lifecycle, the Body of Evidence, the authorization package, and the authorization decision.

sections.heading: Start with the mission, then ask about risk.
sections.body:
The Risk Management Framework (RMF) connects a system’s purpose to the safeguards, evidence, and decisions needed to operate it. Begin with what the organization needs the system to do. Then consider what could happen if information is exposed, changed incorrectly, or unavailable.

An Authorization to Operate (ATO) records a management decision about risk. Installing security tools or finishing a checklist does not make that decision. The authorization package gives the responsible official information to evaluate it.

sections.heading: Everyone contributes. The responsibilities differ.
sections.body:
The system owner is accountable for the system and its package. An Information System Security Manager (ISSM) oversees the security program; an Information System Security Officer (ISSO) supports day-to-day implementation and documentation. Engineers operate safeguards and produce records.

A control assessor evaluates the evidence against the assessment objectives. Common control providers document inherited protections. The Authorizing Official (AO) makes the authorization and risk-acceptance decision within their authority. Local appointments determine the precise division of work.

sections.heading: Follow the claim all the way to the decision.
sections.body:
The Body of Evidence contains the records supporting how the system is secured and operated. The authorization package brings the decision-relevant material together: the plans, assessment reports, outstanding actions, executive summary, and supporting references required by the authority.

A reviewer should be able to move from a requirement to its implementation, to evidence, to an assessment result, and finally to the effect on risk. Missing links are questions to resolve, not paperwork to hide.

sections.heading: From a claim to a decision
sections.body:
Claim: “Privileged account changes are logged and reviewed.”

Evidence: The selected-event configuration, a sample event, and the analyst’s review record.

Assessment: The assessor tests the event and checks whether the expected review occurred.

Decision: The AO considers the supported result and any remaining gap in the system’s risk context.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Create a role map for the system owner, ISSM, ISSO, engineers, control assessor, common control provider, and Authorizing Official (AO). Identify applicable privacy responsibilities.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Given a missing test result and an unresolved risk, identify who supplies evidence, who assesses it, and who has authority to accept the risk.

quizzes.question: The team installed a SIEM and completed its checklist. What comes next?
answers: Treat the system as authorized.
Support implementation claims with assessment evidence and the required risk review.
Replace the SSP with screenshots of the SIEM.
quizzes.explanation: Security tools support control implementation. The assessor evaluates the evidence, and the AO makes the authorization decision.

lessons.title: 02 · Prepare and define the system
lessons.summary: Establish what is being authorized, why it exists, and which organizational and system preparation decisions must be made before documentation expands.

sections.heading: Describe the work the system supports.
sections.body:
Identify the mission, stakeholders, information owners, and dependencies before choosing documents. Record who needs the system, what work it enables, and what service interruption or misuse would affect.

Preparation also happens at the organizational level: risk tolerance, common controls, resources, roles, and oversight influence each system’s approach. Prepare is explicit in NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2.

sections.heading: Draw the boundary, then test the assumptions.
sections.body:
An authorization boundary identifies the system being evaluated. It is more than a subnet diagram. Consider management interfaces, hosting infrastructure, shared services, information flows, and dependencies.

A component outside the boundary can still affect risk. Document its relationship and the responsible party. Do not use a boundary choice to make a difficult dependency disappear.

sections.heading: Identify the governing direction.
sections.body:
Record the authority, relevant policies, adopted control versions, required reviewers, and expected deliverables. Clarify which protections are system-specific, inherited, or shared.

An inherited-control claim needs an identified provider and applicable evidence. In the Inside the Network practice system, transfers across the air gap remain manual and human-controlled.

sections.heading: Resolve a shared-service question
sections.body:
Question: Is the virtualization host covered by this package?

Record: Identify the host, its administrator, and the systems it supports.

Resolve: Document whether it is inside the boundary or provided through a documented external/common service.

Prove: Keep the architecture, inventory, and responsibility record consistent.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Draft a mission statement, boundary diagram, asset list, data flow narrative, stakeholder register, and assumptions log. Record the governing authority, approved standards, overlays, and review expectations. Check each information flow in your narrative against the connection map in Inside the Network, which shows every permitted, pending, and denied rule for a system.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Explain whether a shared service, hypervisor, management path, or offline update transfer is inside the boundary, external, or inherited, and identify supporting responsibility evidence.

quizzes.question: A service sits outside the boundary but provides identity for the system. What should the package do?
answers: Ignore it because it is external.
Assume all of its controls are inherited.
Document the dependency, responsibilities, and applicable assurance evidence.
quizzes.explanation: Being outside a boundary does not remove a dependency or establish inheritance.

lessons.title: 03 · Categorize information and impacts
lessons.summary: Justify confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts using information types and mission consequences. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

sections.heading: Evaluate the consequences for each objective.
sections.body:
Confidentiality concerns inappropriate disclosure. Integrity concerns unauthorized or improper change. Availability concerns reliable access when needed. Categorization starts with information types and the consequences for the mission.

Different objectives can have different impacts. Record the reasoning and applicable methodology; an isolated network alone does not decide the result.

sections.heading: Write a rationale another person can review.
sections.body:
Explain the information processed, the people or mission affected, the potential consequences, and the justification for each impact determination. Capture assumptions and the required approval.

If a system’s mission changes, revisit the rationale. Repeating an inherited label without understanding its basis does not make the categorization defensible.

sections.heading: Apply the right categorization authority.
sections.body:
Federal and national security system contexts do not use identical selection rules. Determine which requirements apply before choosing a baseline or overlay. Consider privacy applicability explicitly.

The optional Secure By Design exercise uses Moderate confidentiality, Low integrity, and Low availability as its stated planning input. That example must not be imposed on another system or treated as an authorization result.

sections.heading: A dependency changes the discussion
sections.body:
Initial rationale: An internal service is needed for routine business support.

New information: A mission process now depends on timely access to it.

Review: Reevaluate availability consequences under the applicable categorization method.

Update: Record the rationale and route it for the required review.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Prepare a categorization worksheet with information types, impact rationale, mission dependencies, approval routing, and privacy considerations. Document the methodology required by the system’s authority.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Defend a changed availability impact after a new mission dependency. Explain why an air gap alone does not establish a low impact level or eliminate risk.

quizzes.question: Does an air gap determine the system’s impact level?
answers: No. Mission consequences and the applicable categorization method determine the rationale.
Yes. It always makes confidentiality Low.
Yes. It eliminates integrity risk.
quizzes.explanation: Isolation is a design characteristic. It does not replace the mission and information impact analysis.

lessons.title: 04 · Select and tailor controls
lessons.summary: Translate the approved categorization and applicable requirements into a justified, assignable control set. Distinguish the control catalog from a selected baseline.

sections.heading: A catalog is not the same as a selected control set.
sections.body:
NIST SP 800-53 describes security and privacy controls. A baseline provides a starting set under an applicable selection method. Overlays and authority-specific requirements can change that starting point.

SP 800-53B provides federal baselines; a national security or SAP selection also requires the applicable CNSS and program direction. Keep these contexts distinct.

sections.heading: Make tailoring decisions visible.
sections.body:
Record why a control is added, adjusted, or considered not applicable and who must approve that decision. Resolve organization-defined parameters such as roles, frequencies, and time periods using the governing direction.

Do not mark a requirement not applicable merely because it is difficult to implement. A reviewer needs both the rationale and its authorized disposition.

sections.heading: Allocate work before asking for evidence.
sections.body:
Identify the owner of each implementation. Distinguish system-specific controls, common controls supplied by a provider, and hybrid controls with shared responsibility.

A Security Control Traceability Matrix (SCTM) can connect the selected requirement, parameter values, ownership, implementation, evidence, assessment result, and associated risk. Its exact format follows local requirements.

sections.heading: An inheritance claim needs support
sections.body:
Claim: “Account management is inherited.”

Question: Which provider performs which part of the requirement?

Evidence: Provider documentation, applicable assessment information, and local responsibilities.

Record: An allocation that separates inherited activities from the system team’s work.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Start a Security Control Traceability Matrix (SCTM). Record control revision, applicability, tailoring rationale, organization-defined parameters, owner, and system-specific, common, or hybrid allocation.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Resolve a proposed not-applicable control and an inherited-control claim using evidence and the required approval path. Pin the selected control and assessment-procedure versions.

quizzes.question: A team calls a difficult control not applicable. What is missing?
answers: A tool screenshot.
A justified applicability decision and the required approval.
A shorter control identifier.
quizzes.explanation: Tailoring must follow the governing process and preserve the rationale.

courses.title: Body of Evidence
courses.subtitle: Document, demonstrate, and assess the network
courses.description: Develop the Body of Evidence for the same Inside the Network build. Write the System Security Plan, connect implementation to proof, organize evidence, and assess findings and residual risk for authorization review.

materials.title: Interactive authorization course
materials.description: Lessons, evidence examples, and the capstone.

materials.title: Full training catalog · Word
materials.description: Edition 1.4 · 12 modules

materials.title: Body of Evidence examples and starters
materials.description: Ten examples with editable Markdown and CSV starters.

lessons.title: 05 · Write the system security plan
lessons.summary: Write a System Security Plan (SSP) that describes the actual system and explains how selected controls are implemented.

sections.heading: Describe the system that actually exists.
sections.body:
The System Security Plan (SSP) identifies the system, its environment, responsible parties, dependencies, and how selected controls are implemented. Keep it consistent with the inventory and architecture.

Describe implemented safeguards and clearly identify planned work. A future improvement should not appear as if it already operates.

sections.heading: Make the implementation understandable.
sections.body:
Explain who performs an activity, what they do, where it applies, when it happens, and which records support the claim. Use the exact selected requirements and parameters as the basis.

“We comply with policy” leaves essential questions unanswered. A useful statement describes the actual process and links to evidence without claiming more than the evidence supports.

sections.heading: Connect the supporting plans.
sections.body:
Configuration, access, incident response, contingency, media, privacy, and other applicable plans describe supporting processes. Connect them to the SSP rather than copying inconsistent versions of the same procedure into several places.

Record the owner, version, and review status of each reference. A plan is evidence of intended process; records and tests help show that the process is carried out.

sections.heading: Improve a vague implementation statement
sections.body:
Before: “Audit logs are reviewed according to policy.”

Better: Identify the assigned reviewer, covered event sources, approved review schedule, exception process, and review record.

Check: Does the scope match the selected requirement and actual source inventory?

Link: Point to the configuration, sample events, and completed review records.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Draft SSP sections for the boundary, system components, roles, and selected controls. Write statements covering who performs the activity, what happens, where it occurs, when it happens, and the supporting evidence.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Replace a vague “compliant with policy” statement with a specific implementation narrative. Reconcile it with the diagrams, inventory, and inheritance record.

quizzes.question: Which SSP statement is most useful?
answers: “The organization is fully compliant.”
“A security product is installed.”
A specific description of the activity, owner, scope, frequency, and evidence.
quizzes.explanation: A defensible implementation statement gives reviewers something concrete to examine, interview about, and test.

lessons.title: 06 · Connect implementation to proof
lessons.summary: Collect technical and operational evidence that addresses the selected requirement and can support an assessment.

sections.heading: Capture the configuration and its context.
sections.body:
A configuration export or hardening checklist is useful when the reviewer can identify the system, setting, scope, version, and collection time. Retain the review or validation record as appropriate.

A passing automated check has a defined scope. Manual checks, applicability decisions, and technical limitations still need attention.

sections.heading: Operational records show whether a process happens.
sections.body:
Logs, scan reports, incident tickets, access reviews, and backup test records support different claims. Connect each item to the question it can answer.

The optional examples use Splunk, Tenable, and Trellix records. Equivalent records can support the exercise. Owning a named product does not itself establish that the selected control is effective.

sections.heading: Coverage is part of evidence quality.
sections.body:
Check whether all relevant systems were included, credentials worked, data was current, and the collection method was appropriate. Preserve collection failures rather than silently excluding them.

Explain what the evidence cannot show. A vulnerability scan does not demonstrate every control, and a backup job success message does not by itself prove recovery.

sections.heading: A clean scan with a coverage problem
sections.body:
Report: The scan reports no critical findings.

Inspection: Authenticated checks failed for two in-scope hosts.

Conclusion: The report does not support a complete credentialed assessment of those hosts.

Follow-up: Correct access, rerun the intended checks, and retain the original coverage limitation.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Collect configuration exports, a reviewed hardening checklist, scan coverage, log review records, and a recovery-test result. Use Splunk, Tenable, and Trellix examples or equivalent supplied training records.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Explain what each item proves and leaves untested. Identify a failed authenticated scan, an unreviewed alert, and a configuration screenshot that lacks system or time context.

quizzes.question: A scan reports no findings, but credentials failed. What can you conclude?
answers: All required checks passed.
The available result is limited; credentialed coverage must be resolved.
No evidence needs to be retained.
quizzes.explanation: The absence of reported findings is not proof that intended checks ran successfully.

lessons.title: 07 · Organize the Body of Evidence
lessons.summary: Make evidence easy to retrieve, trace, and maintain across system changes and assessment cycles.

sections.heading: Give each record a stable identity.
sections.body:
An evidence index lets a reviewer locate a record without relying on a folder name or someone’s memory. Record its identifier, title, scope, owner, collection date, version, and location.

Use a naming convention that is easy to maintain. Protect and retain evidence according to the applicable requirements.

sections.heading: Trace objectives, not just filenames.
sections.body:
Link evidence to the relevant requirement and assessment objective. Keep the implementation statement and assessment conclusion connected to the same scope.

One item may support several objectives, and one objective may need several items. Record the limits of each relationship.

sections.heading: Keep current and historical evidence distinct.
sections.body:
When a system changes, identify which claims and records are affected. Keep version history so a reviewer can understand what was assessed at a particular time.

A current filename on an old screenshot does not make the evidence current. Record collection and review dates separately when they mean different things.

sections.heading: A broken link in the package
sections.body:
Index: EV-003 is listed as proof of current privileged event coverage.

Record: The export predates a new management host.

Gap: The record cannot support the updated coverage claim.

Action: Collect the missing evidence and reconcile the SSP, source inventory, and assessment scope.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Create a master evidence index and link each selected control objective to the implementation, supporting record, owner, collection date, system scope, document version, and review status.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Find stale evidence, a missing record, and a mismatch between the SSP and an exported configuration. Record the gap and its effect on the assessment.

quizzes.question: A screenshot predates a major configuration change. What is the best next step?
answers: Rename it with today’s date.
Leave it because the control number matches.
Review its applicability and obtain current evidence for the changed scope.
quizzes.explanation: Evidence must be relevant to the implementation and time period being assessed.

lessons.title: 08 · Plan and perform assessment
lessons.summary: Turn implementation claims into assessable objectives and distinguish a planned test from an observed result.

sections.heading: Agree on what will be assessed.
sections.body:
The assessment plan describes the objectives, scope, methods, objects, responsibilities, schedule, and practical constraints. Address the required assessor independence and approval path.

Select methods and coverage appropriate to the requirement and risk. Document sampling decisions instead of leaving them implicit.

sections.heading: Use examine, interview, and test deliberately.
sections.body:
Examine records and configurations. Interview people responsible for the process. Test the capability or behavior when appropriate. These methods answer different questions and can complement one another.

Capture the expected result, actual observation, evidence references, and limitations. Follow the adopted SP 800-53A procedures and authority-specific instructions.

sections.heading: Report the result the evidence supports.
sections.body:
The Security Assessment Report (SAR) communicates what was assessed and the resulting findings. Connect each conclusion to the relevant objective, observed result, and supporting evidence.

Unsupported objectives remain unresolved. Document remediation and retests without erasing the original finding or disguising a limitation as a successful result.

sections.heading: Test a privileged account-change event
sections.body:
Plan: Specify the permitted event, relevant sources, expected record, and review process.

Observe: Generate the event in the lab and inspect collection and review records.

Evaluate: Compare observations to each selected objective.

Report: Preserve the result, scope, evidence references, and any coverage gap.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Draft a Security Assessment Plan with objectives, methods, objects, scope, sampling rationale, responsibilities, and schedule. Execute sample procedures and prepare a Security Assessment Report (SAR) excerpt. Include negative tests: run the six attempts in the Inside the Network attack drill, record each expected and observed result in the Operational verification column of the network traffic matrix, and cite the matrix in your SAR excerpt.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Link each conclusion to the assessment objective, evidence, actual observation, and limitation. Record unsupported objectives rather than treating a lack of evidence as a successful test.

quizzes.question: A required assessment objective has no supporting evidence. Should it be marked satisfied?
answers: No. Record the gap and resolve it through the assessment process.
Yes, if the owner expects it to work.
Yes, if another control passed.
quizzes.explanation: Assessment conclusions require support for the relevant objective.

lessons.title: 09 · Manage findings and residual risk
lessons.summary: Translate weaknesses into mission-relevant risk and an accountable response. Explain the difference between technical severity and contextual risk.

sections.heading: Translate the weakness into mission risk.
sections.body:
A finding identifies a weakness or unmet objective. Risk analysis considers the threat, exposure, consequences, existing safeguards, and remaining uncertainty in the system’s context.

Technical severity helps inform prioritization, but it is not the complete risk determination. Explain the mission impact and the reasoning behind the proposed response.

sections.heading: Write an action that can be managed.
sections.body:
A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) records the weakness, affected scope, responsible owner, planned actions, dates, resources, dependencies, and closure criteria.

“Fix soon” is not a milestone. A useful milestone describes a verifiable action and a target date, with a clearly accountable owner.

sections.heading: Verify the correction before closing the record.
sections.body:
Link the corrective action to the original finding. Retest the relevant condition and retain the result. Track delays and changed assumptions through the required review process.

A POA&M is a management record; it does not itself accept risk or grant permission to operate. Those decisions follow the responsible authority’s process.

sections.heading: Make a logging finding actionable
sections.body:
Weakness: SBD-MGMT01, a management host, is missing from verified audit collection.

Response: Restore approved collection and update source coverage records.

Milestones: Confirm configuration, test the selected event, and verify the assigned review process.

Closure: Retain the successful retest and reconcile the SSP, evidence index, and SAR disposition.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Create a risk analysis record and Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) entry with the weakness, affected assets and controls, owner, planned milestones, target dates, resources, status, and closure criteria.

sections.heading: Prove
sections.body: Prioritize two findings with different exposure and mission impact. Preserve the original result, document remediation, and require verification before claiming closure.

quizzes.question: Does adding a finding to a POA&M mean its risk has been accepted?
answers: Yes, automatically.
Only if the spreadsheet has a due date.
No. Risk acceptance follows the authorized decision process.
quizzes.explanation: Tracking a weakness and accepting its risk are different actions.
